docs.title: What Is S3 Storage? S3 vs Local Storage for Your Applications
What Is S3 Storage? S3 vs Local Storage for Your Applications
docs.text: Your application lets users upload invoices and profile pictures. The easy solution is to save them in a folder like /var/app/uploads. It works perfectly, until you add a second server, move to containers, or lose the disk. This post explains S3 object storage, how it differs from local storage, and how to choose.

docs.title: What is S3?
docs.text:
Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) launched in 2006 as a service to store files over HTTP. Its API became so popular that "S3" now also means a protocol: dozens of products, cloud and on-premises, speak the same S3 API. Your code doesn't care whether it talks to AWS, MinIO in your data centre, or Ceph on OpenShift.

S3 is object storage:

Term Meaning Example Bucket A top-level container with its own permissions and settings orders-documents Object A file plus its metadata, stored as one unit the PDF bytes + Content-Type: application/pdf Key The object's unique name inside the bucket invoices/2026/11/inv-1042.pdf Metadata Key/value info attached to an object x-amz-meta-customer-id: 42

There are no real folders: invoices/2026/ is just a key prefix that consoles display as a folder. You don't open, seek and append to objects like files; you PUT a whole object, GET it back, or DELETE it, over HTTPS.

aws s3 mb s3://orders-documents
aws s3 cp inv-1042.pdf s3://orders-documents/invoices/2026/11/inv-1042.pdf
aws s3 ls s3://orders-documents/invoices/2026/11/

docs.title: The three kinds of storage
docs.text:
Block storage File storage Object storage (S3) Looks like A raw disk (/dev/sdb) A shared folder (NFS, SMB) Buckets of objects over HTTP Examples Local SSD, SAN, AWS EBS, VMware VMDK NFS, Windows file share, AWS EFS AWS S3, MinIO, Ceph RGW, Azure Blob* Access One server at a time (mounted) Many servers via a mount Any client, anywhere, via API Edit part of a file Yes Yes No, replace the whole object Scale One volume's size One file server/cluster Practically unlimited Best for Databases, OS disks Legacy apps sharing files Uploads, backups, media, logs, data lakes

*Azure Blob and Google Cloud Storage have their own APIs, with S3-compatible options/gateways.

docs.title: Local storage vs S3 for your application
Local storage (disk on the app server)
docs.text:
Path target = Path.of("/var/app/uploads", fileName);
Files.copy(upload.getInputStream(), target);
  • Simple, fast, no extra service, works offline.
  • Tied to one server. Add a second instance behind a load balancer and half of the users get 404 for files saved on the other node.
  • Containers lose it. A pod's filesystem disappears on restart unless you add a persistent volume, and a ReadWriteOnce volume blocks scaling to many replicas.
  • Backup, replication, encryption and lifecycle are your job.
  • The disk fills up at 3 a.m.

docs.title: S3 object storage
docs.text:
s3.putObject(PutObjectRequest.builder()
        .bucket("orders-documents")
        .key("invoices/2026/11/inv-1042.pdf")
        .contentType("application/pdf")
        .build(),
    RequestBody.fromInputStream(upload.getInputStream(), upload.getSize()));
  • Stateless apps. Any instance can read any file, so you can scale horizontally and restart pods freely. This is exactly what containers and Kubernetes need.
  • Durability. Data is replicated across disks/servers/zones (AWS advertises 99.999999999% durability).
  • Built-in features: versioning, encryption at rest, lifecycle rules (move to cheaper storage, delete after N days), object lock for compliance, replication between sites.
  • Pre-signed URLs: let browsers upload/download directly with a time-limited link, so big files never pass through your app server.
  • Network latency on every access; not suitable for random-access workloads like databases.
  • No partial updates or file locking; "rename" is copy + delete.
  • Costs: storage, requests and especially egress (data out) in public clouds.

docs.title: Side-by-side
docs.text: Question Local disk S3 Multiple app instances share files? No (needs NFS) Yes Survives server/pod loss? Only with backups/RAID Yes, replicated Max capacity Disk size Practically unlimited Latency Microseconds Milliseconds Serve files directly to users Through your app or Nginx Pre-signed URL / CDN Versioning & retention DIY Built in Running cost Hardware you already have Per GB + requests (+ egress) Good for Temp files, caches, single-server apps, databases User uploads, documents, media, backups, logs, exports

docs.title: S3-compatible products
docs.text:
Product Where it runs Notes AWS S3 AWS The original; storage classes from Standard to Glacier Deep Archive MinIO Anywhere (binary, Docker, Kubernetes) Very popular for on-prem and dev environments Ceph RGW On-prem clusters Also provides block and file storage OpenShift Data Foundation OpenShift Ceph + NooBaa, gives buckets via ObjectBucketClaim Cloudflare R2, Wasabi, Backblaze B2 Cloud S3 API, low or zero egress fees Google Cloud Storage / Azure Blob GCP / Azure Native APIs; S3 interoperability options

Try it locally in one command:

docker run -d --name minio -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001 \
  -e MINIO_ROOT_USER=admin -e MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD=change-me-please \
  quay.io/minio/minio server /data --console-address ":9001"

Open http://localhost:9001, create a bucket, and point your app's S3 client at http://localhost:9000 with path-style access enabled.

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
1. Store the key in your database, not the file. Keep invoices/2026/11/inv-1042.pdf in the invoice table; never put binary files in the DB.
  2. Keep buckets private. Serve downloads with short-lived pre-signed URLs or through a CDN, never by making the bucket public.
  3. Use least-privilege credentials per application (one bucket, only the actions it needs), and IAM roles / workload identity instead of static keys where possible.
  4. Turn on versioning and lifecycle rules for important data, plus encryption at rest.
  5. Make the endpoint configurable (S3_ENDPOINT, S3_BUCKET), so the same code works with MinIO in dev and AWS or Ceph in production.

docs.title: When local storage is still right
docs.text:
• Databases, message brokers and search indexes (they need block storage).
  • Temporary processing files you delete after the request.
  • A single-server internal tool with a solid backup.
  • Caches that can be rebuilt.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
Local disk is a place on one server; S3 is a service any server can reach. If your application keeps user files and you ever want more than one instance, containers, or real durability, put those files in S3-compatible object storage and keep only temporary data locally.

Related: Containers vs traditional deployment · What is Nginx? (it can proxy and cache S3/MinIO downloads too)

docs.title: Understanding Containers: Containers vs Traditional Deployment
Understanding Containers: Containers vs Traditional Deployment
docs.text: "It works on my machine" is probably the most expensive sentence in software. Containers exist to make sure that what works on your machine works the same way in test and production. This post explains what a container actually is, how it differs from installing apps on servers or virtual machines, and when each approach makes sense.

docs.title: Three ways to run an application
1. Bare metal: install directly on a server
docs.text:
You install Java, Nginx, the app and its libraries straight onto the operating system of a physical server.

  • Maximum performance, nothing in between.
  • One server = usually one purpose; scaling means buying hardware.
  • Apps share the same libraries; upgrading Java for one app can break another.
  • Servers drift: after two years nobody knows exactly what is installed.

docs.title: 2. Virtual machines (VMs)
docs.text:
A hypervisor (VMware ESXi, KVM, Hyper-V) splits one physical server into many virtual ones. Each VM runs a full guest operating system with its own kernel.

  • Strong isolation, run Windows and Linux side by side.
  • Snapshots, live migration, better hardware use.
  • Each VM carries a whole OS: gigabytes of disk, RAM for the kernel, minutes to boot, and one more OS to patch.

docs.title: 3. Containers
docs.text:
A container packages the application with everything it needs (runtime, libraries, config defaults) into an image, and runs it as an isolated process on a shared Linux kernel. No guest OS, no hypervisor.

  • Megabytes instead of gigabytes; starts in seconds.
  • The same image runs on a laptop, in CI, in test and in production.
  • Dozens of containers per host, each with its own dependencies.
  • Weaker isolation than VMs (shared kernel), and you need new skills and tools.

docs.title: What a container really is
docs.text:
A container is not a small VM. It is a normal Linux process with three kernel features around it:

Feature What it does Namespaces Give the process its own view of PIDs, network, mounts, hostname and users, so it thinks it is alone on the machine cgroups Limit and measure CPU, memory and I/O (this is what --memory=512m uses) Union / overlay filesystem Stack read-only image layers plus a thin writable layer on top

You can see this yourself: run a container and look for its process on the host.

docker run -d --name web nginx:stable-alpine
ps aux | grep "nginx: master"      # it's just a process on the host

docs.title: Images vs containers
docs.text:
• An image is a read-only template, built from a Dockerfile, stored in a registry (Docker Hub, Quay, GHCR, Nexus, Harbor).
  • A container is a running instance of an image. You can start ten containers from one image.
Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre          # base image: OS libraries + Java runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/orders-api.jar app.jar   # your application
EXPOSE 8080
USER 1001                            # don't run as root
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

docker build -t orders-api:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 orders-api:1.0

That image now contains exactly Java 21 and your JAR, on any host that has a container runtime. (Not sure what JRE means here? See JDK vs JRE vs JVM.)

docs.title: Side-by-side comparison
docs.text: Bare metal Virtual machine Container Isolation unit Physical server Full OS with own kernel Process with namespaces Size Whole server GBs MBs to a few hundred MBs Start time Minutes (boot) Minutes Seconds or less Density per host 1 Tens Hundreds Isolation strength Physical Strong (hardware virtualization) Good, shared kernel Portability Low Medium (image formats differ) High (OCI standard) Config drift High Medium Low (immutable images) OS patching Per server Per VM Rebuild the image from an updated base Run Windows apps on Linux host No Yes No (containers share the host kernel type)

docs.title: Containers in production: orchestration
docs.text:
One container on a laptop is easy. Hundreds across many servers need an orchestrator that schedules containers, restarts them when they crash, scales them, and routes traffic:

  • Kubernetes: the industry standard.
  • Red Hat OpenShift: Kubernetes with security, routing, registry and CI built in (see OpenShift is not just Kubernetes).
  • Docker Compose: for a single host, development and small setups.

Containers also change how apps should behave. They should be stateless (keep files in object storage, not on local disk: see S3 vs local storage), read config from environment variables, log to stdout, and expose health checks.

docs.title: Common myths
docs.text:
• "Containers are lightweight VMs." No kernel, no boot, no hypervisor: they are processes.
  • "Containers are secure by default." Not if you run them as root with every capability. Use non-root users, minimal base images and image scanning. OpenShift enforces much of this.
  • "Docker = containers." Docker popularised them, but images follow the open OCI standard; Podman, containerd and CRI-O run the same images.
  • "Containers replace VMs." In most companies, containers run on VMs. They solve different problems and work well together.

docs.title: When traditional deployment is still the right call
docs.text:
• Legacy apps that expect a full OS, hard-coded paths, or GUI access.
  • Heavy, stateful databases where a dedicated, tuned VM is simpler to operate.
  • Windows desktop software or licences tied to a machine.
  • Very small teams with one or two stable apps and no appetite for an orchestrator.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
Bare metal gives raw power, VMs give strong isolation, and containers give speed, density and "build once, run anywhere". For new services and APIs, containers on Kubernetes or OpenShift are the default today; for legacy and heavy stateful systems, a well-managed VM is still a fine answer.

Try it yourself: run Nginx in a container with the Docker option of How to install Nginx.

docs.title: What Is Git? And GitHub vs GitLab vs Bitbucket (and Others) Compared
What Is Git? And GitHub vs GitLab vs Bitbucket (and Others) Compared
docs.text: Every developer uses Git, but many people mix up Git (the tool) and GitHub (a website that hosts Git repositories). This post explains what Git is and why it won, then compares the platforms built around it so you can choose the right one for your team.

docs.title: What is version control?
docs.text:
Without version control, projects end up like this:

report-final.docx
report-final-v2.docx
report-final-v2-ahmed-fixes.docx
report-final-REALLY-final.docx

A version control system (VCS) records every change to your files: who changed what, when and why. You can go back to any earlier version, see exactly what changed between two versions, and let several people work on the same code without overwriting each other.

docs.title: What is Git?
docs.text:
Git is a free, open-source, distributed version control system. Linus Torvalds wrote it in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel source code, and it is now used by almost every software team.

"Distributed" is the key word. With older, centralized systems (SVN, TFVC, CVS) the history lives on one server, so you need that server to commit or look at history. With Git, every clone is a full copy of the repository with its entire history. You can commit, branch, diff and read logs offline, and push to a shared server when you are ready.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Centralized [Centralized - SVN]
      S[(Server<br/>full history)] --- D1[Dev: working copy]
      S --- D2[Dev: working copy]
    end
    subgraph Distributed [Distributed - Git]
      R[(Remote<br/>full history)] --- G1[(Dev: full history)]
      R --- G2[(Dev: full history)]
      G1 -.-> G2
    end

docs.title: Why we use Git
docs.text:
• History and blame. git log and git blame tell you why a line exists, which is gold when debugging a production issue a year later.
  • Branches are cheap. Creating a branch takes milliseconds, so every feature, fix or experiment gets its own branch, and main stays stable.
  • Safe collaboration. Merges and pull/merge requests let teams review code before it lands.
  • Undo almost anything. Revert a bad commit, restore a deleted file, or find the commit that introduced a bug with git bisect.
  • It drives automation. CI/CD pipelines, GitOps (Argo CD, Flux) and infrastructure as code all start from a Git push.
  • Speed and integrity. Most operations are local; every commit is identified by a hash of its content, so history can't be silently corrupted.

docs.title: The core ideas in five minutes
docs.text:
Concept What it means Repository A project folder plus its full history (the hidden .git folder) Working tree → Staging area → Commit Edit files, choose what to include with git add, save a snapshot with git commit Commit A snapshot with an author, date, message and a unique SHA hash Branch A movable pointer to a commit (main, feature/login) Merge / Rebase Two ways to combine the work of two branches Remote Another copy of the repo, usually on GitHub/GitLab (origin) Push / Pull / Fetch Send commits to a remote, or get commits from it Pull Request / Merge Request A platform feature (not Git itself) to review and discuss a branch before merging

A typical day:

git switch -c feature/login        # new branch
# ...edit code...
git add src/LoginController.java
git commit -m "Add login endpoint"
git push -u origin feature/login   # then open a Pull/Merge Request

docs.title: Git vs GitHub: the important difference
docs.text: Git is the tool. GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are services that host Git repositories and add collaboration features around them: web UI, pull requests, code review, issues, CI/CD, permissions, security scanning. Your repository works the same way with any of them, so you can move a repo from one to another with a single git push --mirror.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
The largest platform (owned by Microsoft), home of most open-source projects.

  • Strengths: biggest community, GitHub Actions CI/CD with a huge marketplace, Copilot, Dependabot, code scanning, Codespaces, GitHub Pages (this site runs on it).
  • Self-hosted: yes, GitHub Enterprise Server (paid).
  • Best for: open source, public portfolios, teams that want the richest ecosystem.

docs.title: GitLab
docs.text:
A complete DevSecOps platform in one application, with an open-source core.

  • Strengths: built-in CI/CD that many consider the best integrated pipeline engine, a container registry, package registry, security scanning, issue boards, environments. The free Community Edition can be self-hosted.
  • Self-hosted: yes, free (CE) or paid (EE). Very common in banks and government on-prem.
  • Best for: companies that must keep code on their own servers, or want one tool from commit to deploy.

docs.title: Bitbucket
docs.text:
Atlassian's Git hosting, tightly connected to Jira and Confluence.

  • Strengths: Jira integration (branches and commits linked to tickets), Bitbucket Pipelines.
  • Self-hosted: Bitbucket Data Center (Server edition reached end of life in 2024).
  • Best for: teams already using Jira and Confluence.

docs.title: Others worth knowing
docs.text:
• Azure DevOps Repos: part of Azure DevOps (Boards, Pipelines, Artifacts); common in Microsoft-centric enterprises.
  • Gitea / Forgejo: lightweight, open-source, self-hosted. A single binary that runs on a Raspberry Pi.
  • AWS CodeCommit: AWS closed it to new customers in 2024, so don't start new projects on it.
  • Gerrit: code review focused, used by Android and other large projects.

docs.title: Comparison table
docs.text: GitHub GitLab Bitbucket Azure DevOps Gitea / Forgejo Owner Microsoft GitLab Inc. Atlassian Microsoft Community Free private repos Yes Yes Yes (small teams) Yes (5 users) Yes (self-host) Built-in CI/CD GitHub Actions GitLab CI/CD Pipelines Azure Pipelines Gitea/Forgejo Actions Self-hosted option Enterprise Server (paid) CE free / EE paid Data Center (paid) Azure DevOps Server Free, open source Container registry Yes (GHCR) Yes No (use another) Azure Artifacts / ACR Yes Issue tracking Issues, Projects Issues, Epics, Boards Jira Azure Boards Issues Review name Pull Request Merge Request Pull Request Pull Request Pull Request Open source itself No Core (CE) yes No No Yes Strongest at Community, ecosystem, AI tools All-in-one DevSecOps, on-prem Jira integration Microsoft stack Small, simple, self-hosted

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
• Open source or personal portfolio? → GitHub.
  • Code must stay on your own servers (bank, government, telecom)? → GitLab self-managed (or GitHub Enterprise Server if budget allows).
  • Your company lives in Jira? → Bitbucket, or GitHub/GitLab with the Jira integration.
  • Microsoft / Azure enterprise? → Azure DevOps or GitHub Enterprise.
  • Home lab or small team on a tiny server? → Gitea or Forgejo.

Whichever you pick, the skills transfer: it is all Git underneath.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
Git gives you history, branching and safe collaboration; the platforms add the web, the reviews and the automation around it. Learn Git well first, and switching platforms later is just a remote URL.

Next: How to install Git on Windows, macOS and Linux and set it up properly in five minutes.

docs.title: What Does LTS Mean? Long-Term Support Explained
What Does LTS Mean? Long-Term Support Explained
docs.text: You go to download Java, Node.js or Ubuntu and there are two big buttons: one says LTS, the other has a higher version number. Which one should you pick? This post explains what LTS means, why it exists, and how to choose a version for production systems.

docs.title: LTS in one sentence
docs.text:
LTS (Long-Term Support) is a release that the vendor promises to maintain with security and bug fixes for a long, published period (usually years), without adding breaking changes.

Regular releases (often called feature, current, interim or mainline) get new features first, but are only supported until the next release comes out, often just a few months later.

docs.title: Why LTS exists
docs.text:
Upgrading software in a company is expensive: test, certify, schedule downtime, update documentation, retrain people. Banks, governments and hospitals can't do that every six months.

LTS gives them a deal: "Stay on this version for years. We'll keep it secure and stable. You upgrade when you're ready, from one LTS to the next."

timeline
    title Java: LTS vs feature releases
    2021 : Java 17 LTS
    2022 : Java 18 : Java 19
    2023 : Java 20 : Java 21 LTS
    2024 : Java 22 : Java 23
    2025 : Java 24 : Java 25 LTS

docs.title: LTS vs non-LTS
docs.text: LTS release Regular / feature release Support period Years (2 to 10+) Until the next release (weeks to months) Updates Security and bug fixes only New features + fixes Stability High, battle-tested Newest, less proven Upgrade pressure Low Must upgrade often to stay supported Vendor/tool certification Usually certified Often not Best for Production, enterprise Trying new features, dev, hobby projects

docs.title: Real-world examples
docs.text:
Product LTS scheme Examples Java (OpenJDK) A feature release every 6 months; every 2 years one is LTS 8, 11, 17, 21, 25 are LTS; 22, 23, 24 are not Ubuntu Every 2 years in April (YY.04); 5 years standard support, up to 12 with Ubuntu Pro 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS; 24.10 and 25.04 are interim (9 months) Node.js Even major versions become LTS; odd ones never do 20, 22, 24 LTS; 23 and 25 are "Current" only Windows Server LTSC (Long-Term Servicing Channel): 5 years mainstream + 5 extended Windows Server 2022, Windows Server 2025 RHEL Each major version supported for ~10 years RHEL 8, RHEL 9, RHEL 10 Nginx Stable (even minor) vs mainline (odd minor): same idea, different name 1.28 stable, 1.29 mainline Kubernetes No LTS: each minor version supported ~14 months; vendors (OpenShift EUS, AKS LTS) add longer support OpenShift EUS releases (even minors) Spring Boot No "LTS" label: open-source support ~13 months per minor; commercial support longer Plan regular minor upgrades

Always check the date, not just the label

"LTS" doesn't mean forever. Java 8 and Ubuntu 18.04 were LTS too, and now they are past their free support. Look up the end-of-life (EOL) date. https://endoflife.date is a great one-stop reference.

docs.title: Support phases you will see
docs.text:
Many vendors split LTS into phases:

  1. Active / mainstream support: bug fixes, security fixes, sometimes small improvements.
  2. Maintenance / extended support: critical security fixes only, sometimes paid.
  3. End of life (EOL): no more fixes. Running it means accepting known, unpatched vulnerabilities, and usually failing security audits.

docs.title: How I choose a version for production
docs.text:
1. Default to the latest LTS that your frameworks and tools support (e.g. Java 21 or 25 with Spring Boot 3.x, Node.js 22/24, Ubuntu 24.04, RHEL 9/10, Windows Server 2025).
  2. Check the ecosystem. Is your app server, database driver, monitoring agent or vendor product certified on it?
  3. Avoid a brand-new LTS on day one for critical systems; wait for the first few patch releases.
  4. Plan the next upgrade now. Put the EOL date in the team calendar and upgrade one LTS to the next well before it.
  5. Keep patching inside the LTS. LTS isn't "install and forget": apply its updates (21.0.4 → 21.0.9) regularly; that's the whole point.

Use non-LTS releases for learning, side projects, or when you truly need a new feature and can commit to upgrading every few months.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
LTS is a promise of stability and security for a known period. For anything that runs your business, pick the current LTS, keep it patched, and know its end-of-life date.

Related reading:

  • JDK vs JRE vs JVM: which Java to install, and why LTS matters there
  • How to install Nginx: choosing between stable and mainline

docs.title: What Is Nginx and Why Do We Use It?
What Is Nginx and Why Do We Use It?
docs.text: If you open the HTTP response headers of a random website, there is a good chance you will see Server: nginx. Nginx (pronounced "engine-x") sits in front of a huge share of the web. This post explains what it is, what problems it solves and why it is usually the first thing a request hits in a production stack.

docs.title: Nginx in one sentence
docs.text:
Nginx is a small, fast, event-driven server that accepts HTTP(S) connections and decides what to do with them: serve a file, pass the request to an application, spread it across several servers, cache the answer, or reject it.

It was written by Igor Sysoev in 2004 to solve the C10k problem: how to handle ten thousand concurrent connections on a single machine. Today it comes in two flavours:

Edition Licence Notes Nginx Open Source (nginx.org) BSD-2 What this blog and most companies use NGINX Plus (F5) Commercial Adds active health checks, a live dashboard, JWT auth, support

docs.title: Why it is so fast: event-driven, not thread-per-request
docs.text:
Classic servers such as Apache (prefork / worker MPM) dedicate a process or thread to each connection. Ten thousand slow mobile clients means ten thousand threads, each with its own memory.

Nginx starts one worker process per CPU core. Each worker runs an event loop that handles thousands of connections at once, without blocking on any single one.

flowchart LR
    M[Master process<br/>reads config, manages workers] --> W1[Worker 1<br/>event loop]
    M --> W2[Worker 2<br/>event loop]
    M --> W3[Worker N<br/>event loop]
    C1((client)) & C2((client)) & C3((client)) --> W1
    C4((client)) & C5((client)) --> W2

The practical result: low, predictable memory use and stable latency under heavy load.

docs.title: The six jobs Nginx does for you
1. Web server for static files
docs.text:
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, a React or Angular build: Nginx serves them straight from disk, with sendfile, compression and caching headers.

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name www.example.com;
    root /var/www/site;
    index index.html;
}

docs.title: 2. Reverse proxy
docs.text:
Your Spring Boot, Node.js or Laravel app listens on localhost:8080. Nginx listens on 80/443 and forwards requests to it. The app never faces the internet directly.

location /api/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
}

A forward proxy acts on behalf of clients (a corporate proxy that browsers go through). A reverse proxy acts on behalf of servers. Nginx is almost always used as the second.

docs.title: 3. Load balancer
docs.text:
Run three copies of your app and let Nginx spread the traffic. If one copy dies, Nginx stops sending it requests.

upstream orders_api {
    least_conn;
    server 10.0.0.11:8080;
    server 10.0.0.12:8080;
    server 10.0.0.13:8080 backup;
}

docs.title: 4. TLS (HTTPS) termination
docs.text: Nginx holds the certificate, speaks HTTPS and HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3) with browsers, and talks plain HTTP to the apps on the private network. Certificates live in one place instead of every app.

docs.title: 5. Cache and compression
docs.text: Nginx can cache responses from slow backends (proxy_cache) and gzip text responses, which cuts both latency and backend load.

docs.title: 6. Security gate
docs.text:
Rate limiting, request size limits, IP allow-lists, basic auth, hiding internal headers and blocking paths such as /actuator from the outside: all before a request reaches your code.

limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=login:10m rate=5r/s;

location = /login {
    limit_req zone=login burst=10 nodelay;
    proxy_pass http://orders_api;
}

docs.title: Where Nginx sits in a real architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[Users] -->|HTTPS 443| N[Nginx<br/>TLS, routing, cache]
    N -->|/| FE[Static Angular build]
    N -->|/api| A1[Spring Boot #1]
    N -->|/api| A2[Spring Boot #2]
    N -->|/auth| K[Keycloak]
    A1 & A2 --> DB[(PostgreSQL)]

One public entry point, one certificate, many private services behind it. Kubernetes and OpenShift follow the same idea: the ingress controller (often Nginx itself, or HAProxy on OpenShift) plays this role for the whole cluster.

docs.title: Nginx vs Apache vs HAProxy vs Traefik
docs.text:
Nginx Apache httpd HAProxy Traefik Main strength Web server + reverse proxy Flexible web server, modules Pure load balancing (L4/L7) Auto-config for containers Architecture Event-driven Process/thread (event MPM available) Event-driven Event-driven (Go) Static files Excellent Good No Basic .htaccess per directory No Yes No No Config reload Graceful, no dropped connections Graceful Hitless reload Dynamic, no reload Typical use Front door for web apps and APIs PHP shared hosting, legacy High-traffic TCP/HTTP balancing Docker / Kubernetes labels

My rule of thumb: Nginx when you need a web server and reverse proxy in one; HAProxy when you only need serious load balancing; Traefik when everything is in Docker and you want routes created from labels.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Nginx runs my application." It doesn't run Java or Node.js code. It forwards requests to them. (For PHP it talks to PHP-FPM over FastCGI.)
  • "One Nginx is high availability." A single Nginx is a single point of failure. You need two plus a floating IP; see the HA guide below.
  • "Nginx replaces my API gateway." It covers routing, TLS and rate limits. Full API management (developer portal, subscriptions, analytics) is a different product such as IBM API Connect or Kong.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
Nginx is the front door of your system: it accepts every connection, terminates TLS, protects and routes traffic, and lets your applications focus on business logic. It is fast because it is event-driven, and popular because one small config file replaces a lot of custom code.

Ready to try it?

  • How to install Nginx on Ubuntu, RHEL, Docker or Windows
  • How to configure Nginx as a reverse proxy, load balancer and HA pair
  • Related: Containers vs traditional deployment

docs.title: ACE or Spring Boot? Where integration logic should live
ACE or Spring Boot? Where integration logic should live
docs.text:
Teams that have both IBM App Connect Enterprise and Spring Boot often ask the same question: should this go in ACE or in a service? Choosing badly leads to business rules hidden in integration flows, or hand-written plumbing that ACE would have handled for free.

Here's how I decide.

docs.title: Three layers, three jobs
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    C[Consumers: web, mobile, partners] --> G
    G[IBM API Connect<br/>security, plans, rate limits, analytics] --> S
    G --> A
    S[Spring Boot services<br/>business rules and data] <--> A
    A[IBM App Connect Enterprise<br/>connectivity and transformation] <--> B[ERP · legacy · SMS · IoT · partners]
  • API Connect is the front door: it publishes APIs, applies security policies, plans and rate limits, and gives you analytics.
  • Spring Boot services own the business domain: rules, validation and their own data.
  • App Connect Enterprise owns connectivity: protocols, formats, routing and mediation between systems.

docs.title: Put it in ACE when...
docs.text:
• You are translating between formats (JSON, XML, CSV, fixed-width) or protocols (HTTP, MQ, files, SOAP).
  • You are routing messages to different back ends based on content.
  • You are integrating packaged or legacy systems you can't change.
  • The logic is about how systems talk, not what the business decides.

docs.title: Put it in Spring Boot when...
docs.text:
• The logic is a business rule that the business will want to change and test.
  • It needs its own data and transactions.
  • It requires rich unit tests and fast developer iteration.
  • It is a capability other systems will call, such as "place order" or "calculate entitlement".

docs.title: Warning signs
docs.text: Symptom What it usually means ESQL with hundreds of lines of IF business conditions Domain logic has leaked into the integration layer. A Spring service full of SOAP clients and format mapping You are rebuilding an integration engine by hand. Each consumer calling back ends directly You are missing a gateway: security and visibility suffer. The same transformation copied into many flows Move it into a shared library.

docs.title: A simple rule
docs.text:
If the business would describe it, it belongs in a service. If only an integration engineer would describe it, it belongs in ACE. If it's about who may call what, and how often, it belongs in API Connect.

Keeping those boundaries clean is what lets an enterprise landscape keep growing without turning into a tangle.

docs.title: IBM App Connect Enterprise in practice
IBM App Connect Enterprise in practice
docs.text:
IBM App Connect Enterprise (ACE), the successor of IBM Integration Bus, is the integration engine inside IBM Cloud Pak for Integration. It connects systems that were never designed to talk to each other: an ERP, a REST API, a message queue, a file drop, a partner's SOAP service.

This is the mental model I wish I'd had on day one.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
Concept What it is Message flow A graph of nodes: an input, some processing, one or more outputs. Application / REST API project A deployable unit that groups flows, maps and ESQL. Library / shared library Reusable code and schemas shared by several applications. BAR file The packaged, deployable archive (Broker ARchive). Integration server The runtime process that runs your deployed applications. Policy Externalized configuration: endpoints, credentials, MQ connections.

A typical flow looks like this:

flowchart LR
    I[HTTP Input] --> V[Validate]
    V --> C[Compute: ESQL transform]
    C --> R[HTTP Request: ERP API]
    R --> O[HTTP Reply]
    V -. failure .-> E[Error handler]

docs.title: Transforming messages with ESQL
docs.text:
The Compute node runs ESQL, ACE's language for reading and building message trees. Here a JSON order from a client is reshaped for a back-end system:

CREATE COMPUTE MODULE TransformOrder_Compute
  CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN
  BEGIN
    SET OutputRoot.Properties = InputRoot.Properties;

    SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.orderNumber = InputRoot.JSON.Data.id;
    SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.customerName = InputRoot.JSON.Data.customer.name;
    SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.total = CAST(InputRoot.JSON.Data.amount AS DECIMAL);

    RETURN TRUE;
  END;
END MODULE;

For mapping-heavy work, the graphical Mapping node is often easier to maintain. I use ESQL when the logic has conditions, loops or lookups.

docs.title: Build and deploy from the command line
docs.text:
ACE 12 ships the ibmint tool, which makes builds scriptable and CI/CD friendly:

# Package an application into a BAR file
ibmint package --input-path ./workspace --project OrdersApp \
  --output-bar-file ./build/orders.bar

# Deploy it into an independent integration server's work directory
ibmint deploy --input-bar-file ./build/orders.bar \
  --output-work-directory /home/aceuser/ace-server

The same BAR file is then promoted through every environment, the same way you would promote a container image.

docs.title: Keep configuration out of the code
docs.text: Endpoints, credentials and connection details belong in policies, not hard-coded in flows. On Cloud Pak for Integration, policies and credentials are supplied as configurations attached to the integration runtime. The same BAR then runs in development, test and production with only the configuration changing.

docs.title: Lessons from production
docs.text:
• Design the contract first. Agree on the request, response and error formats before building the flow.
  • Handle errors deliberately. Wire the failure and catch terminals; never let a message disappear silently.
  • Log a correlation ID at every hop so one transaction can be traced across systems.
  • Keep flows small. Several focused flows are easier to test and operate than one huge flow.

Questions or feedback on this post? Contact me.

docs.title: JDK vs JRE vs JVM: What They Are and How They Differ
JDK vs JRE vs JVM: What They Are and How They Differ
docs.text: Three acronyms, one letter apart, and they confuse almost every Java beginner (and some seniors). The short version: the JVM runs Java bytecode, the JRE is what you need to run Java programs, and the JDK is what you need to build them. Here's the long version, with what it means for your laptop, your servers and your container images.

docs.title: From source code to running program
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Hello.java<br/>source code] -->|javac<br/>JDK| B[Hello.class<br/>bytecode]
    B -->|java<br/>JRE| C[JVM]
    C -->|JIT compiles hot code| D[Native machine code<br/>Windows / Linux / macOS]
  1. You write Hello.java.
  2. The compiler javac (part of the JDK) turns it into bytecode (Hello.class), an instruction set for a virtual CPU, not for Intel or ARM.
  3. The JVM loads and runs that bytecode, and its JIT compiler turns frequently used code into real machine code at runtime.

Because every platform has its own JVM, the same .class or .jar runs everywhere: "write once, run anywhere".

docs.title: JVM: Java Virtual Machine
docs.text:
The engine that executes bytecode. It is a specification, with implementations such as HotSpot (the default in OpenJDK) and Eclipse OpenJ9.

What's inside:

Part Job Class loader Finds and loads .class files from JARs and the classpath/module path Bytecode verifier Checks the bytecode is safe before running it Interpreter + JIT compiler Runs bytecode; compiles hot methods to native code (C1/C2 in HotSpot) Garbage collector Frees memory automatically (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah, Parallel…) Runtime memory areas Heap (objects), stacks (per thread), metaspace (class metadata)

The JVM is also why tuning flags look like -Xmx2g, -XX:+UseZGC or -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75: they configure the virtual machine, not your program.

The JVM is not just for Java

Kotlin, Scala, Groovy and Clojure also compile to bytecode and run on the same JVM.

docs.title: JRE: Java Runtime Environment
docs.text:
JRE = JVM + the standard class libraries (java.lang, java.util, java.net, java.sql…) and supporting files. It is everything needed to run a Java application, and nothing to build one: no javac, no debugger.

Is the JRE dead?

Since Java 11, Oracle and OpenJDK no longer ship a separate JRE download. The JDK is the standard distribution, and you can build a custom, minimal runtime for your app with jlink. Vendors such as Eclipse Temurin still publish JRE builds (for example the eclipse-temurin:21-jre container image) because they are handy for small images.

docs.title: JDK: Java Development Kit
docs.text:
JDK = JRE + development tools. Install it on any machine where you write, compile or build Java.

Tool What it does javac Compiles .java to .class java Launches the JVM jar Packages classes into a JAR javadoc Generates API documentation jshell Interactive Java REPL jdb Command-line debugger jlink, jpackage Build a custom runtime / native installer jcmd, jstack, jmap, jfr Diagnose running JVMs: thread dumps, heap dumps, flight recordings

docs.title: Side-by-side
docs.text:
JVM JRE JDK What it is Execution engine Runtime environment Development kit Contains Class loader, JIT, GC, memory JVM + class libraries JRE + compiler & tools Can run Java apps Not alone (needs the libraries) Yes Yes Can compile Java No No Yes (javac) Who needs it Comes inside the JRE/JDK Servers / containers that only run apps Developers, CI build agents

Nested: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM.

docs.title: OpenJDK, Oracle JDK, Temurin… which one?
docs.text:
OpenJDK is the open-source project where Java is developed. Many vendors build and support it; they are functionally almost identical and all pass the same compatibility tests (TCK).

Distribution Vendor Notes Eclipse Temurin Adoptium (Eclipse) Free, popular default, official Docker images Red Hat build of OpenJDK Red Hat Included with RHEL/OpenShift subscriptions; UBI images Amazon Corretto AWS Free, long support, tuned for AWS Microsoft Build of OpenJDK Microsoft Used across Azure Oracle JDK Oracle Check the licence terms for production use Azul Zulu Azul Free builds + commercial support GraalVM Oracle Adds native-image compilation (fast startup)

My default: Temurin on laptops and generic servers, Red Hat build of OpenJDK on RHEL and OpenShift, and always an LTS version (17, 21, 25). Why LTS matters is in What does LTS mean?.

docs.title: What to install where
docs.text:
• Developer laptop: a JDK (via SDKMAN!, winget install EclipseAdoptium.Temurin.21.JDK, or sudo dnf install java-21-openjdk-devel). Check with java -version and javac -version.
  • CI build agent: a JDK, same major version as production.
  • Production server / container: a JRE-sized runtime is enough. Use a multi-stage build: JDK to compile, JRE to run.
# Build with the JDK…
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests

# …run with the JRE: a smaller image with fewer tools for an attacker to use
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY --from=build /src/target/*.jar /app/app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

More on why containers change how we ship Java in Containers vs traditional deployment.

docs.title: Quick check: what do I have installed?
docs.text:
java -version      # runtime (JRE or JDK)
javac -version     # only works if a JDK is installed
echo $JAVA_HOME    # which installation tools like Maven use

openjdk version "21.0.9" 2025-10-21 LTS
OpenJDK Runtime Environment Temurin-21.0.9+10 (build 21.0.9+10-LTS)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM Temurin-21.0.9+10 (build 21.0.9+10-LTS, mixed mode, sharing)

The third line is your JVM (HotSpot "Server VM"), the second is the runtime, and LTS tells you it's a long-term-support release.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
• JVM runs bytecode.
  • JRE = JVM + libraries, enough to run Java.
  • JDK = JRE + tools, needed to build Java.

Install a JDK where you write code, ship a JRE-sized runtime where you run it, and pick an LTS version from a vendor you trust.

docs.title: OpenShift Routes: Edge, Passthrough and Re-encrypt TLS Explained
OpenShift Routes: Edge, Passthrough and Re-encrypt TLS Explained
docs.text: A Route is how traffic from outside the cluster reaches your app on OpenShift. Creating one takes a single command; choosing where TLS ends is the decision that actually matters, for security, for features and for debugging. This post explains the three options and when I use each.

docs.title: How a request reaches your pod
docs.text:
Client ──► DNS *.apps.cluster.example.com
       ──► Router (HAProxy pods, the default IngressController)
       ──► Service  (selects pods by label)
       ──► Pod      (ready endpoints only)

The router runs HAProxy and watches every Route in the cluster. A wildcard DNS record points *.apps.<cluster-domain> at it, so any Route under that domain works without touching DNS. For a custom domain, point a CNAME at the router.

docs.title: Plain HTTP
docs.text:
oc expose service orders-api
oc get route orders-api
# orders-api-orders-dev.apps.cluster.example.com

Fine for a quick test. For anything real, pick one of the TLS types below.

docs.title: 1. Edge: TLS ends at the router
docs.text:
Client ══TLS══► Router ──HTTP──► Pod

oc create route edge orders-api \
  --service=orders-api \
  --hostname=orders.example.com \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key --ca-cert=ca.crt \
  --insecure-policy=Redirect
  • Without --cert, the router uses the cluster's default wildcard certificate.
  • --insecure-policy=Redirect sends http:// traffic to https://.
  • The router can read HTTP, so you get path-based routing, sticky sessions (cookies) and X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto headers.

Use it for: most web apps and APIs, when traffic inside the cluster network is acceptable in plain HTTP.

Spring Boot behind an edge route

Your app sees HTTP, so generated redirects and links may use http://. Set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework (or native) so Spring trusts X-Forwarded-Proto.

docs.title: 2. Passthrough: TLS goes all the way to the pod
docs.text:
Client ══════════TLS══════════► Pod   (router only reads the SNI hostname)

oc create route passthrough orders-api \
  --service=orders-api \
  --hostname=orders.example.com
  • The router never decrypts. It picks the backend using SNI from the TLS handshake.
  • The pod holds the certificate and serves TLS itself.
  • No path routing, no cookies, no forwarded headers: the router cannot see HTTP.

Use it for: mutual TLS where the app must see the client certificate (bank or partner integrations, for example IBM ACE or API gateways doing mTLS), non-HTTP protocols over TLS, and compliance rules that forbid decrypting at the edge.

docs.title: 3. Re-encrypt: TLS at the router, and again to the pod
docs.text:
Client ══TLS══► Router ══TLS══► Pod

oc create route reencrypt orders-api \
  --service=orders-api \
  --hostname=orders.example.com \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key

You get edge features (path routing, headers, cookies) and encryption inside the cluster. The router must trust the pod's certificate. The easy way is a service serving certificate, signed automatically by OpenShift's service CA:

oc annotate service orders-api \
  service.beta.openshift.io/serving-cert-secret-name=orders-api-tls

OpenShift creates the secret orders-api-tls (tls.crt, tls.key) and rotates it. Mount it in the pod and serve HTTPS on 8443. For a re-encrypt route with no destinationCACertificate, the router trusts the service CA automatically.

# Spring Boot: serve HTTPS with the mounted PEM files
server:
  port: 8443
  ssl:
    certificate: /etc/tls/tls.crt
    certificate-private-key: /etc/tls/tls.key

Use it for: regulated environments that require encryption in transit everywhere, while still needing router features.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Edge Passthrough Re-encrypt Where TLS ends Router Pod Router, then new TLS to pod Encrypted inside cluster No Yes Yes Certificate on Router Pod Both Path-based routing Yes No Yes Sticky sessions (cookie) Yes No Yes X-Forwarded-* headers Yes No Yes Client certificate (mTLS) seen by app No Yes No Complexity Low Medium Medium

docs.title: Useful annotations
docs.text:
# Long-running requests (default is 30s)
oc annotate route orders-api haproxy.router.openshift.io/timeout=120s

# Load-balancing algorithm
oc annotate route orders-api haproxy.router.openshift.io/balance=roundrobin

docs.title: Route or Ingress?
docs.text: Both work. If you create a Kubernetes Ingress, OpenShift generates a Route from it, and you can choose the termination with an annotation such as route.openshift.io/termination: reencrypt. I use Ingress when the same manifests must run on other Kubernetes clusters, and Route when I need passthrough, re-encrypt or router annotations without workarounds.

docs.title: "Application is not available"
docs.text:
That page is the router saying: I have a Route, but no ready pod behind it. Check in this order:

oc get endpoints orders-api             # empty? nothing is ready or selected
oc get pods -l app=orders-api           # are pods Running and READY 1/1?
oc describe svc orders-api              # selector and targetPort match the pod?
oc get route orders-api -o yaml         # spec.to.name and spec.port.targetPort correct?

The usual causes: a failing readiness probe, a selector that does not match the pod labels, or a targetPort that points at the wrong port name. For passthrough and re-encrypt, also check that the pod actually serves TLS on that port.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
• Edge for most apps: simple, full HTTP features.
  • Passthrough when the app must own TLS, especially for mTLS.
  • Re-encrypt when you need router features and encryption everywhere; service serving certificates make it nearly free.

docs.title: Why Your Container Fails on OpenShift (and How to Fix It Properly)
Why Your Container Fails on OpenShift (and How to Fix It Properly)
docs.text: The image runs fine with docker run. It runs fine on your Kubernetes cluster. You deploy it to OpenShift and the pod goes straight into CrashLoopBackOff with Permission denied. The quick fix most people find on the internet is anyuid. Here is why that is usually the wrong fix, and what to do instead.

docs.title: The symptoms
docs.text:
nginx: [emerg] mkdir() "/var/cache/nginx/client_temp" failed (13: Permission denied)

Error: listen EACCES: permission denied 0.0.0.0:80

chown: changing ownership of '/data': Operation not permitted

Different apps, same cause: the image assumes it runs as root (or as one specific user), and on OpenShift it does not.

docs.title: What OpenShift actually does
docs.text:
Every pod is admitted through a Security Context Constraint (SCC). Ordinary workloads get restricted-v2, which:

  • runs the container as a random UID from a range reserved for the project;
  • adds the user to the root group (GID 0), but gives it no root privileges;
  • drops all Linux capabilities and blocks privilege escalation;
  • applies the default seccomp profile.

You can see the range assigned to your project:

oc get namespace orders-dev -o yaml | grep sa.scc
#   openshift.io/sa.scc.uid-range: 1000680000/10000

And check which SCC a running pod received and which user it runs as:

oc get pod orders-api-7d9c-xkq2 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.openshift\.io/scc}{"\n"}'
# restricted-v2
oc rsh orders-api-7d9c-xkq2 id
# uid=1000680000(1000680000) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000680000

So the process is user 1000680000, which owns nothing in the image. Any directory owned by root:root with mode 755 is read-only to it. Ports below 1024 need a capability it does not have.

docs.title: Why not just grant anyuid?
docs.text:
oc adm policy add-scc-to-user anyuid -z default   # please don't

This lets every pod using the default service account in the project run as any user, including root. A container escape now starts from root on the node. On a shared or regulated cluster, it also tends to fail the next security review. And it hides the real problem: the image is not built to run unprivileged, which is a good practice on any platform.

docs.title: The proper fix: build images that run as any user
docs.text:
The rule is simple. Whatever the app needs to write must be owned by group 0 and group-writable. Because the random user is always a member of group 0, it gets access.

FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal

RUN microdnf install -y nginx && microdnf clean all

# 1. Writable paths: group 0 + same permissions as the owner
RUN mkdir -p /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx /run/nginx \
 && chgrp -R 0 /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx /run/nginx /etc/nginx \
 && chmod -R g=u /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx /run/nginx /etc/nginx

# 2. Listen on an unprivileged port. In nginx.conf also set:
#    listen 8080;  and  pid /run/nginx/nginx.pid;
EXPOSE 8080

# 3. A numeric, non-root user (OpenShift will override the UID anyway)
USER 1001

CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

Three habits cover most cases:

  1. chgrp -R 0 <dir> && chmod -R g=u <dir> for every path the app writes to.
  2. Listen on 8080 / 8443, never 80 / 443. The Service and Route map the public port.
  3. Use a numeric USER, never root, and do not chown at runtime.

Ready-made images

Many projects publish unprivileged variants: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged, Bitnami images, and Red Hat UBI images (ubi9/nginx-124, ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime, ubi9/postgresql-16) are built for the random UID out of the box.

docs.title: Volumes
docs.text: For persistent volumes, OpenShift sets an fsGroup from the project range, so the mounted volume is writable by the pod. Do not run an init container that chowns the volume: it needs root and will be rejected.

docs.title: Apps that need a username
docs.text:
A few tools (older Java libraries, SSH, some Python packages) call getpwuid() and crash when the UID has no entry in /etc/passwd. UBI-based images handle this. In your own images you can make /etc/passwd group-writable and add the entry in an entrypoint script:

#!/bin/sh
if ! whoami >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "app:x:$(id -u):0:app user:/app:/sbin/nologin" >> /etc/passwd
fi
exec "$@"

docs.title: When you genuinely need another SCC
docs.text:
Some workloads need more: a vendor image you cannot rebuild, a monitoring agent that reads host files. Then:

  1. Ask OpenShift which SCC would admit the pod:

    oc policy scc-subject-review -f deployment.yaml

  2. Create a dedicated service account and grant the SCC only to it, never to default:

    oc create serviceaccount legacy-app
oc adm policy add-scc-to-user anyuid -z legacy-app
oc set serviceaccount deployment/legacy-app legacy-app

  3. Document why, and add it to the list of exceptions you review regularly.

privileged should stay reserved for platform components such as CSI drivers and node agents.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Writable paths owned by group 0 with g=u permissions
  • App listens on a port above 1024
  • Numeric non-root USER in the Dockerfile
  • No runtime chown, no root init containers
  • Extra SCCs only through a dedicated service account, with a reason

Images that follow these rules run on OpenShift, on vanilla Kubernetes with Pod Security restricted, and on any hardened Docker host. Fixing the image once is cheaper than defending an exception forever.
