docs.title: OpenShift Is Not Just Kubernetes: What You Actually Get
OpenShift Is Not Just Kubernetes: What You Actually Get
docs.text: "OpenShift is just Kubernetes with a Red Hat logo." I hear this often, and it is half true. Every OpenShift cluster is a conformant Kubernetes cluster: your Deployments, Services and ConfigMaps work as they do anywhere else. The difference is everything Red Hat decided you should not have to assemble yourself. This post walks through what those decisions are and when they are worth it.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
Plain Kubernetes gives you an engine. OpenShift gives you the car: engine, brakes, dashboard, seatbelts already fastened. You lose some freedom to pick parts, and you gain a platform that a small team can run in production.

Concern Plain Kubernetes OpenShift Exposing apps over HTTP(S) Choose and install an Ingress controller Routes + HAProxy router, installed Pod security Pod Security Admission, you set the policy SCCs, restricted by default Login & users Bring your own (OIDC, certs…) Built-in OAuth server (LDAP, OIDC, htpasswd) Image registry Install one Integrated registry + ImageStreams Building images External CI BuildConfig (S2I, Docker) in-cluster Monitoring Install Prometheus stack Prometheus + Alertmanager preinstalled Cluster upgrades Distro-specific Cluster Version Operator, one click / one command Node OS Any Linux RHCOS, immutable and managed by the cluster CLI kubectl oc (a superset of kubectl)

docs.title: 1. Projects instead of bare namespaces
docs.text:
A Project is a namespace with extras: a display name, a description, and a template that can attach default quotas, limit ranges and network policies the moment it is created. Developers can be allowed to create their own projects (oc new-project) without being cluster admins.

oc new-project orders-dev --display-name="Orders (dev)"
oc get project orders-dev -o yaml

docs.title: 2. Routes: ingress that is already there
docs.text:
Every cluster ships with an ingress controller (HAProxy) and a wildcard DNS name like *.apps.cluster.example.com. Exposing a service is one command:

oc expose service orders-api                          # plain HTTP
oc create route edge orders-api --service=orders-api  # HTTPS, TLS ends at the router

Routes also support passthrough and re-encrypt TLS, which I cover in OpenShift Routes explained. Standard Ingress objects still work: OpenShift converts them to Routes for you.

docs.title: 3. Secure by default (and why your image breaks)
docs.text:
This is the one that surprises people most. OpenShift does not let containers run as root by default. The restricted-v2 Security Context Constraint (SCC) runs each pod with a random, high user ID taken from a range assigned to the project, drops all Linux capabilities and blocks privilege escalation.

Images from Docker Hub that assume root (write to /var/cache/nginx, bind to port 80) fail on day one. That is a feature: it is the same hardening you should be doing anyway. The full story and the fix are in Why your container fails on OpenShift.

docs.title: 4. Authentication is built in
docs.text:
OpenShift runs its own OAuth server. Point it at LDAP / Active Directory, an OIDC provider such as Keycloak, or GitHub, and users log in to the console and the CLI with their existing accounts. Groups can be synced from LDAP and bound to roles.

oc login --web https://api.cluster.example.com:6443
oc whoami
oc adm groups new platform-admins
oc adm policy add-cluster-role-to-group cluster-admin platform-admins

docs.title: 5. Registry, ImageStreams and Builds
docs.text: The cluster includes an image registry. On top of it, an ImageStream is a pointer to images (internal or external) that can trigger a redeploy when a tag changes. BuildConfigs build images inside the cluster from a Git repo or a binary upload, using Source-to-Image (S2I) or a Dockerfile. You do not have to use them (many teams build in GitLab CI and push to Nexus or Quay), but for small teams they remove a lot of plumbing. I compare the options for Java in Building Spring Boot images for OpenShift.

docs.title: 6. Operators run the cluster, and your middleware
docs.text:
OpenShift is managed by Operators: the Cluster Version Operator upgrades the whole platform, the Machine Config Operator manages node configuration, and so on. The same model is offered to you through OperatorHub: install Kafka (AMQ Streams), databases, Keycloak (Red Hat build of Keycloak), service mesh, GitOps (Argo CD) or IBM Cloud Pak for Integration with a few clicks, and the operator handles day-2 tasks like upgrades and failover.

oc get clusterversion
oc get clusteroperators   # the health of every platform component

docs.title: 7. Observability out of the box
docs.text: Prometheus, Alertmanager and dashboards for the platform are preinstalled. You can enable user workload monitoring to scrape your own apps (for example Spring Boot's /actuator/prometheus) with a ServiceMonitor, no extra Prometheus to run.

docs.title: When OpenShift is worth it
docs.text:
Choose OpenShift when:

  • you run in a regulated environment (banking, government, healthcare) that needs vendor support, certifications and hardened defaults;
  • the team is small and cannot afford to assemble and patch ten components by hand;
  • you run vendor software certified on OpenShift (IBM Cloud Pak, for example);
  • you need the same platform on-prem, in the cloud and at the edge.

Plain Kubernetes (or a managed service) may be enough when:

  • you are cloud-native on a single provider and happy with EKS / AKS / GKE;
  • you want full control over every component;
  • budget is the main constraint (OpenShift is a subscription; OKD is the free upstream).

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
OpenShift's value is not one big feature. It is dozens of decisions already made: secure defaults, integrated login, routing, registry, monitoring and push-button upgrades. If those are decisions your team would otherwise make (and maintain) itself, OpenShift saves real time. If not, plain Kubernetes is a perfectly good engine.

Next in this series: why your container fails on OpenShift, and how to fix it properly.

docs.title: Understanding LDAP: Active Directory vs OpenLDAP and Other Directory Servers
Understanding LDAP: Active Directory vs OpenLDAP and Other Directory Servers
docs.text: Every time you log in to a company laptop, VPN, Jenkins, GitLab or Keycloak with the same username and password, there is very likely an LDAP directory behind it. This post explains what LDAP is, how a directory is organised, and how the main products compare: Active Directory, OpenLDAP, FreeIPA / 389 Directory Server and friends.

docs.title: What is LDAP?
docs.text:
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is an open, standard protocol (version 3, RFC 4511) for reading and writing a directory: a database optimised for many fast reads and few writes, that stores information about users, groups, computers and other resources.

Two things to keep apart:

  • LDAP is the protocol: the language clients use (bind, search, add, modify).
  • A directory server is the product that stores the data and speaks LDAP: Active Directory, OpenLDAP, 389 DS…

What companies use it for:

  • Central authentication: one account for every app ("check this user's password").
  • Authorization: group membership (is alice in cn=devs?).
  • Address book / lookup: email, phone, manager, department.
  • Machine and service info: computers, printers, service accounts.

docs.title: How a directory is organised
docs.text:
Data lives in a tree (the DIT, Directory Information Tree). Each node is an entry with attributes, and is identified by its Distinguished Name (DN), read from the leaf up to the root:

dc=bhry98,dc=local                       ← root (the domain bhry98.local)
├── ou=Users
│   ├── cn=Alice Ahmed                    DN: cn=Alice Ahmed,ou=Users,dc=bhry98,dc=local
│   └── cn=Bob Hassan
└── ou=Groups
    └── cn=devs                           member: cn=Alice Ahmed,ou=Users,dc=bhry98,dc=local
Abbreviation Meaning Example dc Domain component dc=bhry98,dc=local ou Organizational unit (a "folder") ou=Users cn Common name cn=Alice Ahmed uid / sAMAccountName Login name (OpenLDAP / AD) alice objectClass What kind of entry it is (defines allowed attributes) inetOrgPerson, user, group

An entry in LDIF, the text format for LDAP data:

dn: cn=Alice Ahmed,ou=Users,dc=bhry98,dc=local
objectClass: inetOrgPerson
cn: Alice Ahmed
sn: Ahmed
uid: alice
mail: alice@bhry98.local

docs.title: How an application uses LDAP
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as App (Keycloak, Jenkins...)
    participant D as Directory (LDAP server)
    U->>A: username alice + password
    A->>D: BIND as service account
    A->>D: SEARCH (uid=alice) under ou=Users
    D-->>A: DN cn=Alice Ahmed,ou=Users,...
    A->>D: BIND as that DN with alice's password
    D-->>A: Success (or invalidCredentials)
    A->>D: SEARCH groups where member = alice's DN
    A-->>U: Logged in, roles from groups

Try it from any Linux machine with ldapsearch:

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01.bhry98.local \
  -D "svc-ldap@bhry98.local" -W \
  -b "dc=bhry98,dc=local" "(sAMAccountName=alice)" cn mail memberOf

docs.title: LDAP vs LDAPS: always encrypt
docs.text:
Port Traffic LDAP 389 Plain text: passwords in simple binds can be sniffed LDAP + StartTLS 389 Starts plain, then upgrades to TLS LDAPS 636 TLS from the first byte (like HTTPS) Global Catalog (AD only) 3268 / 3269 (SSL) Forest-wide search

Never send passwords over plain 389 in production. Setting up LDAPS on Active Directory is a step-by-step job, covered in How to secure Active Directory with LDAPS.

docs.title: Microsoft Active Directory (AD DS)
docs.text:
Far more than an LDAP server. AD combines LDAP + Kerberos + DNS + Group Policy + replication to manage Windows domains: users log in to Windows PCs, computers get policies, admins use familiar GUI tools.

  • Attributes: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName (alice@bhry98.local), memberOf.
  • Multi-master replication between domain controllers, sites, forests and trusts.
  • Runs on Windows Server only. The default in most enterprises.

docs.title: OpenLDAP
docs.text:
The classic open-source LDAP server (slapd) for Linux.

  • Lightweight, fast and extremely flexible, with custom schemas and overlays (memberOf, password policy).
  • Configured with LDIF (cn=config). Powerful, but there's no built-in GUI and a steep learning curve.
  • Great for Linux-only environments, appliances, and as a backend for other products.

docs.title: 389 Directory Server / FreeIPA / Red Hat IdM
docs.text: 389 DS is Red Hat's open-source LDAP server. FreeIPA (sold as Red Hat Identity Management) builds on it with Kerberos, DNS, a certificate authority, sudo rules, host-based access control and a web UI. Think of it as "Active Directory for Linux". It can also trust an AD forest, so Windows users can log in to Linux servers.

docs.title: Others you'll meet
docs.text:
• Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD): cloud identity for Microsoft 365. Despite the old name it is not an LDAP server (it uses OAuth2/OIDC/SAML); Entra Domain Services adds managed LDAP. More in What is Microsoft Entra ID?.
  • Samba AD DC: an open-source, AD-compatible domain controller on Linux.
  • Apache Directory Server / ApacheDS, OpenDJ / PingDS: Java-based LDAP servers.
  • JumpCloud, Google Cloud Identity (Secure LDAP): directory-as-a-service with LDAP endpoints.
  • Keycloak is not a directory. It uses one: through User Federation it reads users from AD/LDAP and offers modern SSO (OIDC/SAML) to your apps. See How to install Keycloak.

docs.title: Comparison table
docs.text: Active Directory OpenLDAP FreeIPA / Red Hat IdM Entra ID Type Full Windows domain service Pure LDAP server Linux identity suite Cloud identity (IdP) Licence Windows Server licence Open source Open source / RH subscription Microsoft subscription Platform Windows Server Linux/Unix RHEL, Fedora, CentOS Stream SaaS LDAP v3 Yes Yes Yes (389 DS) No (only via Domain Services) Kerberos Built in Separate (MIT/Heimdal) Built in No (cloud Kerberos for hybrid only) Policies for machines Group Policy (Windows) No HBAC, sudo rules (Linux) Intune / Conditional Access Built-in CA AD CS (separate role) No Dogtag CA, built in No Admin UI ADUC, ADAC, PowerShell CLI / 3rd-party (phpLDAPadmin) Web UI + CLI Web portal Best for Windows-centric companies Custom, lightweight Linux directories Linux fleets, AD trusts Microsoft 365, cloud SSO

docs.title: Which one should you choose?
docs.text:
• Mostly Windows PCs and Microsoft software? Active Directory. Nothing else manages Windows as well.
  • Linux servers needing central logins, sudo rules and certificates? FreeIPA / Red Hat IdM, optionally trusted with AD.
  • An app or appliance that just needs a small LDAP backend? OpenLDAP or 389 DS.
  • Cloud-first with Microsoft 365? Entra ID, synced from on-prem AD if you have one (how to set up the sync).
  • Modern web apps and APIs? Put Keycloak in front of your directory and let apps use OIDC instead of talking LDAP directly.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
LDAP is the common language; Active Directory, OpenLDAP and FreeIPA are different servers that speak it, each with its own extras. Whatever you run, keep the directory as the single source of truth for identities, and always use LDAPS.

Next: Secure your Windows Active Directory with LDAPS (Windows Server 2025)

docs.title: What Is Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) and Why Do We Use It?
What Is Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) and Why Do We Use It?
docs.text: If your company uses Outlook, Teams or anything in Azure, you already have Microsoft Entra ID, even if nobody calls it that. Most people still say "Azure AD". In this post I explain what Entra ID actually is, how it is different from the Active Directory running on your domain controllers, and why so many companies end up putting it at the center of their logins.

docs.title: First, the name
docs.text:
Microsoft renamed Azure Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID in 2023. Same product, same tenant, same features. "Entra" is now the family name for Microsoft's identity products:

Product What it does Entra ID The main one: users, groups, sign-in, SSO, MFA, Conditional Access Entra ID Governance Access reviews, joiner/mover/leaver workflows, entitlement management Entra External ID Sign-in for customers and partners (the replacement for Azure AD B2C) Entra Connect / Cloud Sync Tools that copy users from on-premises AD into Entra ID

So when you read an old blog post about "Azure AD Connect" or an "Azure AD tenant", just replace the name with Entra in your head. Nothing else changed.

docs.title: So what is it?
docs.text:
Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service. It keeps a list of your users, groups, devices and applications, and it answers one question all day long:

Is this person who they say they are, and are they allowed into this app right now?

Every time someone signs in to Microsoft 365, the Azure portal, or any app that shows the Microsoft login page, that request goes to Entra ID. It checks the password (or passkey, or Windows Hello), asks for MFA if needed, looks at the device and location, and then hands the app a token that says "this is alice@contoso.com, she is in these groups".

Each company gets its own isolated copy called a tenant, with a default domain like contoso.onmicrosoft.com. You then add your real domain (contoso.com) so users sign in with their normal email address.

docs.title: Entra ID is not "Active Directory in the cloud"
docs.text:
This is the part that confuses most people, me included the first time. The old name made it sound like a domain controller hosted by Microsoft. It is not.

Active Directory (AD DS) Microsoft Entra ID Where it runs Your servers (domain controllers) Microsoft's cloud, nothing to install Built for Windows networks inside an office Web apps, SaaS and mobile over the internet Protocols Kerberos, NTLM, LDAP OpenID Connect, OAuth 2.0, SAML, SCIM Structure Forests, domains, OUs, Group Policy Flat: one tenant, users, groups, admin units Computers Domain join, GPOs Entra join, managed with Intune Can apps use LDAP against it? Yes No Who patches and backs it up You Microsoft

The short version: AD is for the network, Entra ID is for the internet. An old in-house app that does an LDAP bind will not work against Entra ID. A modern SaaS app that wants SAML or OIDC will not talk to your domain controller directly. That is why most companies run both and connect them (more on that below).

What about Entra Domain Services?

If you really need LDAP or Kerberos in Azure for a lifted-and-shifted app, there is a paid add-on called Microsoft Entra Domain Services that gives you managed domain controllers. It is a separate service, not a feature of Entra ID itself.

If LDAP, binds and DNs are new to you, my post Understanding LDAP: Active Directory vs OpenLDAP covers that side.

docs.title: 1. One account for everything (SSO)
docs.text: Users sign in once and get into Microsoft 365, Azure, Salesforce, ServiceNow, GitHub, Jira, Zoom and thousands of other apps from the gallery, plus your own apps through OIDC or SAML. When someone leaves, you disable one account and their access to all of it stops. That alone is the main reason security teams push for it.

docs.title: 2. MFA and passwordless
docs.text: Turning on MFA for every user is a few clicks. You can use the Microsoft Authenticator app, FIDO2 security keys, passkeys or Windows Hello for Business, and slowly move people away from passwords altogether.

docs.title: 3. Conditional Access
docs.text:
This is the feature I find most useful in practice. You write rules like:

  • Admins must always use MFA from a compliant device.
  • Block sign-ins from countries where we have no staff.
  • Finance apps only from company laptops.
  • If the sign-in looks risky, force a password change.

Entra ID checks these rules on every sign-in, not just once at login time on the office network. This is the "zero trust" idea in a form you can actually configure.

docs.title: 4. Access for people outside the company
docs.text: Partners and contractors can be invited as guests (B2B) and sign in with their own company account. No need to create and later forget to delete local accounts for them.

docs.title: 5. It is already there
docs.text: If you pay for Microsoft 365, you already have a tenant and the Free tier of Entra ID. For a lot of companies the question is not "should we buy it" but "should we start using what we already pay for".

docs.title: Licences in one table
docs.text:
Edition You get Typical use Free Users, groups, SSO to apps, basic MFA (security defaults), sync from AD Small companies, anything with Microsoft 365 P1 Conditional Access, dynamic groups, self-service password reset with writeback to AD, Application Proxy Most companies end up here P2 Everything in P1 plus Identity Protection (risk-based sign-in) and PIM (just-in-time admin roles) Stricter security needs

P1 is included in Microsoft 365 E3 and Business Premium, P2 in E5, so check what your licences already cover before buying anything. Prices and bundles change often, so always confirm on Microsoft's licensing page.

docs.title: Hybrid: AD and Entra ID together
docs.text:
Very few companies start fresh in the cloud. The usual setup is:

flowchart LR
    AD["Active Directory<br/>bhry98.local<br/>(source of truth)"] -- "Entra Connect Sync<br/>or Cloud Sync" --> E["Microsoft Entra ID<br/>contoso.com"]
    E --> M["Microsoft 365"]
    E --> A["Azure"]
    E --> S["SaaS apps"]
    AD --> L["File shares, GPO,<br/>old LDAP apps"]

HR creates the user in Active Directory like always. A sync tool copies that user (and a hash of the password hash) to Entra ID, so the same username and password work for both the office network and Microsoft 365. You keep managing people in one place and you don't end up with two passwords per person.

I wrote a full step-by-step guide for this: How to sync Active Directory users to Microsoft Entra ID.

docs.title: Where Keycloak fits
docs.text:
On this blog I write a lot about Keycloak, so a fair question is: Keycloak or Entra ID?

  • Entra ID makes sense when the company already lives in Microsoft 365 and wants a managed service with MFA, Conditional Access and device compliance built in.
  • Keycloak makes sense when you need full control, run on-premises or in OpenShift, cannot send identity data to a public cloud, or want to avoid per-user licence costs.

They also work together. Keycloak can use Entra ID as an external identity provider over OIDC, so employees sign in with their Microsoft account while your apps keep talking to Keycloak.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Microsoft Entra ID is the new name for Azure AD: Microsoft's cloud identity service.
  • It handles sign-in, SSO, MFA and Conditional Access for Microsoft 365, Azure and any app that speaks OIDC, SAML or OAuth 2.0.
  • It is not a domain controller. No LDAP, no Group Policy, no OUs.
  • Most companies run AD and Entra ID side by side and sync users from AD to the cloud.
  • If you have Microsoft 365, you already have it. Start with MFA and SSO, add Conditional Access when you get P1.

docs.title: Running Spring Boot on OpenShift
docs.text: Getting a Spring Boot service to start on OpenShift takes five minutes. Getting it to behave well in production (rolling updates without errors, sensible memory use, configuration per environment) takes a few deliberate choices. This is the checklist I follow.

docs.title: 1. Build an image that runs as any user
docs.text:
OpenShift runs containers with a random, non-root user ID that belongs to the root group. Images that assume root, or write to directories only their owner can write to, fail at startup.

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /src/target/*.jar app.jar
RUN chgrp -R 0 /app && chmod -R g=u /app
USER 1001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

Two details matter here:

  • Port 8080. Ports below 1024 need privileges the container won't have.
  • -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75. The JVM sizes its heap from the container's memory limit, leaving room for metaspace, threads and native memory. Without it you get either a wasted limit or an OOMKilled pod.

Tip

Red Hat's UBI OpenJDK images (ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime) are built for this environment and are a good choice when you need a supported base image.

docs.title: 2. Use Actuator for health probes
docs.text:
Spring Boot Actuator exposes separate liveness and readiness groups. They are enabled automatically when the app detects Kubernetes, and you can turn them on explicitly:

# application.yaml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info

# Deployment
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 20

Keep the liveness check simple. If it depends on the database, a short database outage restarts every pod at once and turns a small incident into a big one.

docs.title: 3. Shut down gracefully
docs.text:
During a rolling update, OpenShift sends SIGTERM to the old pod. Let in-flight requests finish:

server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s

Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds on the pod higher than that timeout.

docs.title: 4. Configuration from the platform
docs.text:
Build one image and promote it through every environment. Everything that changes per environment comes from OpenShift:

What Where URLs, feature flags, log levels ConfigMap as environment variables Passwords, client secrets, keys Secret TLS for the public endpoint Route with edge or re-encrypt termination

Spring's relaxed binding maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to spring.datasource.url, so no code changes are needed.

oc create configmap orders-config --from-literal=SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
oc set env deployment/orders-api --from=configmap/orders-config
oc create route edge orders-api --service=orders-api

docs.title: 5. Set requests and limits
docs.text:
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
  limits:   { memory: 1Gi }

Requests let the scheduler place pods sensibly. A memory limit protects the node. I usually avoid a tight CPU limit for JVM services because throttling slows startup and garbage collection.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Non-root image listening on 8080
  • Heap sized with MaxRAMPercentage
  • Readiness and liveness probes on Actuator
  • Graceful shutdown configured
  • Config in ConfigMaps, secrets in Secrets
  • Resource requests and a memory limit

Questions or feedback on this post? Contact me.

docs.title: Building Spring Boot Images for OpenShift: Dockerfile, S2I or Jib?
Building Spring Boot Images for OpenShift: Dockerfile, S2I or Jib?
docs.text: There are at least four reasonable ways to get a Spring Boot JAR running as an image on OpenShift. They all work. They differ in where the build runs, who controls the base image and how much CI you need. Here is each one with real commands, and how I pick between them.

docs.title: Option 1: Dockerfile, built in CI, pushed to a registry
docs.text:
The most portable approach. GitLab CI (or Jenkins, GitHub Actions) builds the image and pushes it to Nexus, Quay or Harbor; OpenShift only pulls and runs it.

FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21 AS build
USER 0
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package

FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime
COPY --from=build /src/target/*.jar /deployments/app.jar
EXPOSE 8080

# .gitlab-ci.yml (simplified)
build-image:
  image: quay.io/buildah/stable
  script:
    - buildah bud -t $REGISTRY/orders-api:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA .
    - buildah push $REGISTRY/orders-api:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

deploy:
  image: registry.redhat.io/openshift4/ose-cli
  script:
    - oc login --token=$OC_TOKEN --server=$OC_SERVER
    - oc set image deployment/orders-api orders-api=$REGISTRY/orders-api:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA
    - oc rollout status deployment/orders-api

The UBI OpenJDK runtime image runs /deployments/*.jar automatically, works with OpenShift's random UID, and sizes the heap from the container limit.

Good: same image everywhere, full control, no build load on the cluster. Cost: you maintain the CI pipeline and the registry.

docs.title: Option 2: Docker strategy, built inside OpenShift
docs.text:
Same Dockerfile, but OpenShift builds it with a BuildConfig and stores the result in the internal registry.

oc new-build --strategy=docker --binary --name=orders-api
oc start-build orders-api --from-dir=. --follow
oc new-app orders-api                  # first deploy
oc expose service orders-api

Good: no registry or Docker daemon needed outside the cluster. Handy for small teams and disconnected environments. Cost: builds use cluster CPU and memory; the cluster admin may restrict the Docker strategy.

docs.title: Option 3: Source-to-Image (S2I)
docs.text:
No Dockerfile at all. You give OpenShift source code (or a JAR), and a builder image knows how to build and run Java.

From Git:

oc new-app registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21~https://gitlab.example.com/team/orders-api.git \
  --name=orders-api

Or from a JAR you already built:

oc new-build registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21 --binary --name=orders-api
./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
oc start-build orders-api --from-file=target/orders-api.jar --follow

Good: developers only push code; Red Hat maintains the base image, so rebuilding picks up security patches. Cost: less control over the image layout; OpenShift-specific.

docs.title: Option 4: Jib, no Dockerfile and no Docker daemon
docs.text:
Jib, a Maven/Gradle plugin from Google, builds layered images directly from the build tool. Dependencies, resources and classes go in separate layers, so a code change pushes only a few KB.

<plugin>
  <groupId>com.google.cloud.tools</groupId>
  <artifactId>jib-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.4.4</version>
  <configuration>
    <from><image>registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime</image></from>
    <to><image>nexus.example.com:8443/team/orders-api</image></to>
    <container>
      <user>185</user>
      <ports><port>8080</port></ports>
    </container>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

./mvnw compile jib:build -Djib.to.tags=$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

Good: fast incremental builds, reproducible, runs in any CI container without privileges. Cost: Java-only; you still need a registry.

Cloud Native Buildpacks

./mvnw spring-boot:build-image (Paketo Buildpacks) is a fifth option with good defaults. It needs a Docker-compatible daemon at build time, which is often the deciding factor in CI.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Dockerfile in CI Docker strategy S2I Jib Build runs in CI OpenShift OpenShift CI / laptop Needs Dockerfile Yes Yes No No Needs Docker daemon No (Buildah/Kaniko) No No No External registry Yes No No Yes Portable to other K8s Yes Image only Image only Yes Incremental speed Good (layer cache) Good Medium Best Base image patching You You Red Hat You

docs.title: Triggering the deploy
docs.text:
Whatever builds the image, roll it out in one of two ways:

# Explicit: CI sets the new tag (clear audit trail, easy rollback)
oc set image deployment/orders-api orders-api=nexus.example.com:8443/team/orders-api:1.4.2
oc rollout status deployment/orders-api
oc rollout undo deployment/orders-api        # if needed

# Automatic: redeploy when an ImageStream tag changes (in-cluster builds)
oc set triggers deployment/orders-api --from-image=orders-api:latest -c orders-api

docs.title: How I choose
docs.text:
• Team already has GitLab CI and a registry: Dockerfile (or Jib) in CI, oc set image to deploy. Portable, auditable, and the cluster only runs workloads.
  • Small team, no external registry, or a disconnected cluster: binary S2I with the UBI OpenJDK builder. Least to maintain.
  • Many Java microservices with frequent builds: Jib, for layer reuse and speed.

Whichever you choose, the runtime rules stay the same: non-root image, port 8080, probes on Actuator, graceful shutdown. They are all in Running Spring Boot on OpenShift.

docs.title: How to secure Active Directory with LDAPS (Windows Server 2025)
How to secure Active Directory with LDAPS (Windows Server 2025)
docs.text:
Before you start

Read Understanding LDAP: Active Directory vs OpenLDAP if terms like bind, DN or LDAP vs LDAPS are new to you.

By default, applications talk to Active Directory over LDAP on port 389, and a simple bind sends the username and password in plain text across the network. LDAPS wraps the same protocol in TLS on port 636, exactly like HTTPS does for HTTP.

Domain controllers turn on LDAPS automatically as soon as they have a suitable certificate. So the job is really: give every DC a trusted certificate and keep it renewed. The cleanest way is an Enterprise CA with Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) and auto-enrollment.

By the end of this guide you will have:

  • An Enterprise Root CA for bhry98.local
  • Every domain controller auto-enrolled with a server certificate that renews itself
  • LDAPS working on ldaps://dc01.bhry98.local:636 (and the Global Catalog on 3269)
  • Linux, Java and Keycloak clients trusting your CA

docs.title: Lab used in this guide
docs.text:
Host IP OS Role DC01.bhry98.local 10.0.0.10 Windows Server 2025 Domain controller (AD DS + DNS) for bhry98.local CA01.bhry98.local 10.0.0.20 Windows Server 2025 Domain member, will become the Enterprise CA client any Windows 11 / Linux Testing

About the screenshots

The pictures in this guide are illustrations of the Windows Server 2025 dialogs, drawn with the exact values of this lab (bhry98.local, CA01, DC01), so you can compare them with your own screen field by field.

Small lab with only one server?

Microsoft recommends not installing AD CS on a domain controller. In a throw-away lab it works if you run every CA step on DC01, but use a separate server anywhere else.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Notes A working AD domain bhry98.local DC01 promoted, DNS working A second server joined to the domain CA01, for AD CS An account in Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins Needed to install an Enterprise CA Time in sync Kerberos and certificates both fail with clock skew

Check from DC01 that the domain is healthy before you start:

dcdiag /q            # no output = no errors
Resolve-DnsName ca01.bhry98.local

docs.title: Step 1: Install the AD CS role on CA01
docs.text:
Sign in to CA01 as BHRY98\Administrator (an Enterprise Admin).

Server Manager (GUI)PowerShell
  1. Server Manager → Manage → Add Roles and Features.
  2. Installation Type: Role-based or feature-based installation.
  3. Server Selection: CA01.bhry98.local.
  4. Server Roles: check Active Directory Certificate Services, accept Add Features.
  5. Role Services: keep only Certification Authority.
  6. Install, then close the wizard when it finishes.

Server Roles: select Active Directory Certificate Services.

Install-WindowsFeature ADCS-Cert-Authority -IncludeManagementTools

docs.title: Step 2: Configure an Enterprise Root CA
docs.text:
An Enterprise CA is integrated with AD: it publishes its certificate to every domain member, uses certificate templates, and supports auto-enrollment. That is what makes LDAPS automatic.

Server Manager (GUI)PowerShell
  1. Click the flag notification in Server Manager → Configure Active Directory Certificate Services on the destination server.
  2. Credentials: BHRY98\Administrator → Next.
  3. Role Services: check Certification Authority.

  4. Setup Type: Enterprise CA.

    Setup Type: Enterprise CA.

  5. CA Type: Root CA.

  6. Private Key: Create a new private key.
  7. Cryptography: RSA#Microsoft Software Key Storage Provider, key length 4096, hash SHA256.

  8. CA Name: keep the default bhry98-CA01-CA. The suffix is DC=bhry98,DC=local.

    CA Name: the common name your clients will see as the issuer.

  9. Validity Period: 10 years (a root CA should outlive the certificates it issues).

  10. Certificate Database: keep the defaults → Configure.
Install-AdcsCertificationAuthority `
  -CAType EnterpriseRootCA `
  -CACommonName "bhry98-CA01-CA" `
  -CryptoProviderName "RSA#Microsoft Software Key Storage Provider" `
  -KeyLength 4096 `
  -HashAlgorithmName SHA256 `
  -ValidityPeriod Years -ValidityPeriodUnits 10 `
  -Force

Check that the CA is running and which templates it publishes:

Get-Service certsvc
certutil -CATemplates

DomainController: Domain Controller -- Auto-Enroll
KerberosAuthentication: Kerberos Authentication -- Auto-Enroll
DomainControllerAuthentication: Domain Controller Authentication -- Auto-Enroll
WebServer: Web Server -- Access is denied
...

The Kerberos Authentication and Domain Controller templates are published by default and allow the Domain Controllers group to auto-enroll. Both include the Server Authentication purpose and the DC's DNS name, which is exactly what LDAPS needs.

Production PKI

For production, Microsoft's recommended design is an offline standalone root CA plus an online enterprise subordinate CA. The DC side of this guide (Steps 3 to 6) is identical; only the CA setup differs.

docs.title: Step 3: Turn on certificate auto-enrollment for domain controllers
docs.text:
Auto-enrollment makes DCs request and renew their certificates on their own. You only configure it once.

Group Policy (GUI)PowerShell
  1. On DC01, open Group Policy Management (gpmc.msc).
  2. Forest → Domains → bhry98.local → Group Policy Objects → right-click Default Domain Controllers Policy → Edit.
  3. Go to Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Public Key Policies.
  4. Open Certificate Services Client - Auto-Enrollment:
    • Configuration Model: Enabled
    • Check Renew expired certificates, update pending certificates, and remove revoked certificates
    • Check Update certificates that use certificate templates
  5. OK.

Auto-Enrollment in the Default Domain Controllers Policy.

# AEPolicy = 7: enabled + renew/remove + update templates (same as the GUI settings)
Set-GPRegistryValue -Name "Default Domain Controllers Policy" `
  -Key "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Cryptography\AutoEnrollment" `
  -ValueName AEPolicy -Type DWord -Value 7

docs.title: Step 4: Enroll the domain controller certificate
docs.text:
On DC01 (and later every other DC), apply the policy and trigger enrollment now instead of waiting up to 8 hours:

gpupdate /force
certutil -pulse

Check the computer's personal certificate store:

Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My |
  Where-Object { $_.EnhancedKeyUsageList.FriendlyName -contains "Server Authentication" } |
  Format-List Subject, DnsNameList, Issuer, NotAfter, Thumbprint

Subject     :
DnsNameList : {DC01.bhry98.local, bhry98.local, BHRY98}
Issuer      : CN=bhry98-CA01-CA, DC=bhry98, DC=local
NotAfter    : 11/22/2027 10:15:42 AM
Thumbprint  : 4F2A...

Or graphically with certlm.msc → Personal → Certificates:

DC01 now holds certificates from bhry98-CA01-CA with Server Authentication in Intended Purposes.

What makes a certificate usable for LDAPS

  • The DC's FQDN (DC01.bhry98.local) in the Subject or Subject Alternative Name
  • Server Authentication (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1) in Enhanced Key Usage
  • A private key in the Local Computer store
  • Issued by a CA the DC and the clients trust

docs.title: Step 5: Make AD load the certificate
docs.text:
The DC picks up a valid certificate automatically, normally within minutes or after a reboot. To load it right now without a reboot, ask AD to refresh its server certificate:

@"
dn:
changetype: modify
add: renewServerCertificate
renewServerCertificate: 1
-
"@ | Set-Content -Encoding ascii $env:TEMP\ldaps-renew.ldf

ldifde -i -f $env:TEMP\ldaps-renew.ldf

Connecting to "DC01.bhry98.local"
Logging in as current user using SSPI
Importing directory from file "C:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\ldaps-renew.ldf"
Loading entries..
1 entry modified successfully.

docs.title: From the domain controller or a Windows client
docs.text:
Check the port is listening:

Test-NetConnection dc01.bhry98.local -Port 636     # TcpTestSucceeded : True
Test-NetConnection dc01.bhry98.local -Port 3269    # Global Catalog over SSL

Then use ldp.exe (installed with the AD DS tools):

  1. Run ldp.exe.
  2. Connection → Connect…
  3. Server: dc01.bhry98.local (the FQDN, not the IP, because it must match the certificate), Port: 636, check SSL → OK.
  4. Optional: Connection → Bind with a domain account to test a login.

Success: Host supports SSL, SSL cipher strength = 256 bits and Established connection.

docs.title: From Linux
docs.text:
First export the CA certificate (Step 7), then:

# See the certificate chain the DC presents
openssl s_client -connect dc01.bhry98.local:636 -CAfile bhry98-CA.pem -showcerts </dev/null \
  | grep -E "subject=|issuer=|Verify return code"

subject=
issuer=DC=local, DC=bhry98, CN=bhry98-CA01-CA
Verify return code: 0 (ok)

# Search the directory over LDAPS
LDAPTLS_CACERT=bhry98-CA.pem ldapsearch -H ldaps://dc01.bhry98.local:636 \
  -D "administrator@bhry98.local" -W \
  -b "dc=bhry98,dc=local" "(sAMAccountName=administrator)" cn memberOf

Done. bhry98.local answers LDAPS on 636 with a trusted, auto-renewing certificate.

docs.title: Step 7: Make clients trust your CA
docs.text:
Domain-joined Windows machines trust the Enterprise CA automatically (it is published in AD). Everything else needs the CA certificate.

Export it on CA01:

certutil -ca.cert C:\bhry98-CA.cer      # DER format

Copy bhry98-CA.cer to your clients, then:

Linux (RHEL / Ubuntu)Java / Spring BootKeycloak 
openssl x509 -inform der -in bhry98-CA.cer -out bhry98-CA.pem

# RHEL / Rocky / Fedora
sudo cp bhry98-CA.pem /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/
sudo update-ca-trust

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo cp bhry98-CA.pem /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/bhry98-CA.crt
sudo update-ca-certificates

# Into a dedicated truststore
keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias bhry98-ca -file bhry98-CA.cer \
  -keystore truststore.p12 -storetype PKCS12 -storepass changeit

java -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=truststore.p12 \
     -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit -jar app.jar

# Keycloak 25+: add the PEM to the system truststore used by Keycloak
bin/kc.sh start --truststore-paths=/opt/keycloak/conf/truststores/bhry98-CA.pem ...

Then in User federation → Add LDAP provider:

Field Value Vendor Active Directory Connection URL ldaps://dc01.bhry98.local:636 Bind DN svc-keycloak@bhry98.local Users DN OU=Users,DC=bhry98,DC=local

Click Test connection and Test authentication. See How to install Keycloak for the Keycloak setup itself.

docs.title: Step 8: Harden it by turning off plain-text LDAP
docs.text:
LDAPS only helps if clients actually use it. Once your apps are switched to ldaps://:

  1. Find who still uses insecure binds. On each DC, raise LDAP interface logging and watch Directory Service event 2889 (each client doing an unsigned or clear-text bind) and 2887 (daily summary):

    Set-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Diagnostics" `
  -Name "16 LDAP Interface Events" -Value 2

  2. Require LDAP signing (Windows Server 2025 already requires it by default on new deployments; on older or upgraded domains set it yourself). In the Default Domain Controllers Policy → Security Options:

    • Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements → Require signing
    • Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements → When supported, then Always once 2889 events are gone

  3. Firewall: allow 636 and 3269 from the networks that need them; block 389/3268 from outside the server network if nothing legitimate uses them.

  4. Monitor certificate expiry. Auto-enrollment renews it, but alert on Directory Service event 1220 (LDAP over SSL will be unavailable…) and on certificates close to expiry.

Test before enforcing

Requiring signing or channel binding breaks old devices (printers, scanners, appliances, old Java apps) that use plain simple binds on 389. Use the 2889 events to find and fix them first.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
ldp with SSL: Cannot open connection / error 0x51

No usable certificate on the DC. Re-check Step 4 (Server Authentication EKU, FQDN, private key), run certutil -pulse, then Step 5. Look for event 1220 in the Directory Service log.

Works with the FQDN, fails with the IP address

Expected: the certificate is issued to DC01.bhry98.local, not to 10.0.0.10. Always use the DNS name in connection URLs.

Linux / Java: unable to get local issuer certificate or PKIX path building failed

The client doesn't trust bhry98-CA01-CA. Import the CA certificate (Step 7) into the OS trust store or the Java truststore your app actually uses.

No certificate appears after certutil -pulse

Check the GPO reached the DC (gpresult /r /scope computer), that the CA is online (certutil -ping), and that the Domain Controllers group has Enroll and Autoenroll on the template (Certificate Templates console certtmpl.msc → template → Security).

Two DCs, only one works

Each DC needs its own certificate. Run Steps 4 to 6 on every domain controller.

docs.title: How to sync Active Directory users to Microsoft Entra ID
How to sync Active Directory users to Microsoft Entra ID
docs.text:
Before you start

New to Entra ID? Read What is Microsoft Entra ID and why do we use it? first.

Most companies already have their users in an on-premises Active Directory and now also need them in Microsoft Entra ID for Microsoft 365, Azure and SaaS apps. Creating every user twice by hand doesn't scale and ends with two passwords per person. The fix is to let AD stay the place where you manage people and have a sync tool copy them to Entra ID.

In this guide I use Microsoft Entra Connect Sync (the tool people still call "Azure AD Connect") with password hash sync, which is what I'd pick for most setups. At the end there is a section on the lighter Entra Cloud Sync agent and when to use it instead.

By the end of this guide you will have:

  • Users from selected OUs in bhry98.local showing up in Entra ID
  • The same username and password working on-premises and in Microsoft 365
  • A sync running every 30 minutes on its own
  • A clear process for new users, changes and leavers

docs.title: Lab used in this guide
docs.text:
Host IP OS Role DC01.bhry98.local 10.0.0.10 Windows Server 2025 Domain controller (AD DS + DNS) SYNC01.bhry98.local 10.0.0.30 Windows Server 2025 Domain member, will run Entra Connect Sync Entra tenant contoso.onmicrosoft.com with the custom domain contoso.com verified

Replace contoso.com with your own public domain everywhere below. It's the same domain lab as my LDAPS guide, so if you followed that one you already have DC01.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph onprem["On-premises"]
        DC["DC01<br/>AD DS"]
        S["SYNC01<br/>Entra Connect Sync"]
    end
    E["Microsoft Entra ID<br/>contoso.com"]
    DC -- "LDAP read<br/>(MSOL_ account)" --> S
    S -- "HTTPS 443<br/>outbound only" --> E
  • Entra Connect reads users, groups and contacts from AD, applies your filters, and writes them to Entra ID. Only outbound HTTPS, no inbound ports to open.
  • AD is the source of authority. A synced user is edited in AD, not in the Entra portal. Most fields are greyed out in the cloud.
  • With password hash sync, Entra ID gets a hash of the AD password hash (never the password itself), so users sign in to the cloud without the request touching your DCs.
  • Every 30 minutes it runs a delta sync that only sends what changed.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Notes A working AD domain bhry98.local, healthy (dcdiag /q shows nothing) A Windows Server 2016 or newer, domain-joined SYNC01. Not a domain controller (supported, but I'd avoid it) An Entra tenant with your domain verified Entra admin center → Entra ID → Domain names → Add custom domain, then add the TXT record it gives you Entra account with the Hybrid Identity Administrator (or Global Administrator) role Cloud-only account, admin@contoso.onmicrosoft.com, with MFA AD account in Enterprise Admins Only used during setup to create the sync service account Outbound HTTPS 443 from SYNC01 To the Microsoft endpoints; TLS 1.2 enabled Fewer than about 100,000 objects Otherwise use a full SQL Server instead of the built-in SQL Express LocalDB

Clean up AD first

Whatever is in the OUs you pick will end up in the cloud. Duplicate mail or proxyAddresses values, users with empty mail, and old test accounts cause errors later. Microsoft's IdFix tool scans AD and lists these problems. Run it once before you start.

docs.title: Step 1: Give users a routable UPN
docs.text:
Users sign in to Entra ID with their UPN. alice@bhry98.local can't be used in the cloud because nobody can verify .local on the internet. If you sync as-is, users get alice@contoso.onmicrosoft.com instead, which nobody wants to type.

Add contoso.com as a UPN suffix on DC01, then move the users to it:

PowerShellGUI 
# 1. Add the suffix to the forest
Get-ADForest | Set-ADForest -UPNSuffixes @{Add = "contoso.com"}

# 2. See who still has the old suffix
Get-ADUser -SearchBase "OU=Staff,DC=bhry98,DC=local" -Filter * |
    Where-Object UserPrincipalName -like "*@bhry98.local" |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, UserPrincipalName

# 3. Change them (test on one OU first)
Get-ADUser -SearchBase "OU=Staff,DC=bhry98,DC=local" -Filter * |
    Where-Object UserPrincipalName -like "*@bhry98.local" |
    ForEach-Object {
        $new = $_.UserPrincipalName -replace "@bhry98\.local$", "@contoso.com"
        Set-ADUser $_ -UserPrincipalName $new
    }
  1. Active Directory Domains and Trusts → right-click the root → Properties.
  2. Alternative UPN suffixes: add contoso.com → OK.
  3. In Active Directory Users and Computers, open a user → Account tab → pick @contoso.com in the drop-down next to the logon name.

Users can still log in to Windows as BHRY98\alice as before. Only the UPN changes.

Make UPN and email match

Life is easier when alice@contoso.com is both the UPN and the email address. Fill the mail attribute too, because Exchange Online and many apps read it.

docs.title: Step 2: Decide which OUs to sync
docs.text:
Don't sync the whole domain. Service accounts, disabled users and the built-in Users container don't belong in the cloud. In this lab I sync two OUs:

DC=bhry98,DC=local
├── OU=Staff          ← sync
├── OU=Groups         ← sync
├── OU=ServiceAccounts
└── CN=Users          (built-in, not synced)

You choose these OUs in the wizard in Step 4, and you can change them later.

docs.title: Step 3: Download and install on SYNC01
docs.text:
Sign in to SYNC01 as a domain admin.

  1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center (entra.microsoft.com), go to Entra ID → Entra Connect → Connect Sync and download the latest installer. Microsoft moved the download there; older links to the Download Center point at outdated versions.
  2. Run MicrosoftEntraConnectSyncSetup.msi (the exact file name changes between releases).
  3. Accept the licence terms → Continue.

docs.title: Step 4: Run the wizard with custom settings
docs.text:
Express settings syncs the entire forest with password hash sync. It works, but I prefer Customize so I can choose the OUs.

  1. Install required components: leave the defaults (built-in SQL Express LocalDB, auto-created service account) → Install.
  2. User sign-in: select Password Hash Synchronization and tick Enable single sign-on (Seamless SSO, so domain-joined PCs on the network don't ask for a password again).
  3. Connect to Microsoft Entra ID: sign in with admin@contoso.onmicrosoft.com and approve MFA.
  4. Connect your directories: forest bhry98.local → Add Directory → Create new AD account, enter BHRY98\Administrator (Enterprise Admin). The wizard creates a low-privilege account named MSOL_xxxxxxxx that it uses from now on.
  5. Microsoft Entra sign-in configuration: you should see contoso.com as Verified and bhry98.local as Not Added. Keep USER PRINCIPAL NAME as the attribute. Since all users are already on @contoso.com from Step 1, tick Continue without matching all UPN suffixes to verified domains.
  6. Domain and OU filtering: choose Sync selected domains and OUs and tick only Staff and Groups.
  7. Uniquely identifying your users: keep the defaults. Users are matched by UPN and the source anchor is ms-DS-ConsistencyGuid. Don't change this unless you know why.
  8. Filter users and devices: Synchronize all users and devices.
  9. Optional features: leave Password hash synchronization ticked. If you have Entra ID P1, also tick Password writeback so users can reset their AD password from the cloud.
  10. Enable single sign-on: enter domain admin credentials when asked. This creates a computer account called AZUREADSSOACC in AD.
  11. Ready to configure: tick Start the synchronization process when configuration completes → Install.

The first full sync starts right away. On a small domain it takes a few minutes.

Staging mode

The same screen has Enable staging mode. A server in staging mode imports and calculates everything but doesn't write to Entra ID. Install a second server like that and you have a ready standby if SYNC01 dies.

docs.title: Step 5: Check that users arrived
docs.text:
Entra admin centerPowerShell (Microsoft Graph)

Entra ID → Users → All users. Add the column On-premises sync enabled. Your AD users show Yes, cloud-only admins show No.

Entra ID → Entra Connect → Connect Sync shows the last sync time and whether password hash sync is healthy.

Install-Module Microsoft.Graph -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "User.Read.All","Organization.Read.All"

# When did the tenant last sync?
Get-MgOrganization | Select-Object OnPremisesSyncEnabled, OnPremisesLastSyncDateTime

# Is this user coming from AD?
Get-MgUser -UserId alice@contoso.com `
    -Property DisplayName,UserPrincipalName,OnPremisesSyncEnabled,OnPremisesSamAccountName |
    Select-Object DisplayName, UserPrincipalName, OnPremisesSyncEnabled, OnPremisesSamAccountName

Then do the real test: open https://myapps.microsoft.com in a private browser window and sign in as alice@contoso.com with her AD password.

docs.title: Step 6: Run and monitor sync from PowerShell
docs.text:
Everything below runs on SYNC01 in an elevated PowerShell (the ADSync module is installed with Entra Connect).

# Status of the scheduler: is it on, when is the next run?
Get-ADSyncScheduler

# Push changes now instead of waiting up to 30 minutes
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta

# After changing filters or rules: full sync
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial

# Pause the scheduler during maintenance, then turn it back on
Set-ADSyncScheduler -SyncCycleEnabled $false
Set-ADSyncScheduler -SyncCycleEnabled $true

For errors on single objects, open Synchronization Service Manager (installed with Entra Connect). The Operations tab lists every run; click a run with warnings to see which user failed and why. The usual suspect is a duplicate proxyAddresses or UPN.

docs.title: Managing users day to day
docs.text:
Once sync is on, the rule is simple: change users in AD, never in the cloud. Here is what each common task looks like.

Task Do this in AD What happens in Entra ID New employee Create the user in OU=Staff with a @contoso.com UPN Appears after the next sync. Assign the Microsoft 365 licence (or use group-based licensing) Name, title, department, manager Edit the user in AD Updated on the next sync Password change User changes it with Ctrl+Alt+Del or you reset it in AD Synced within about 2 minutes (password sync runs on its own schedule) Add to a group Add to a group inside OU=Groups Group membership updated in Entra ID Employee leaves Disable the account in AD Sign-in blocked after the next sync. Revoke sessions in Entra to cut access right away Delete Delete in AD (or move out of synced OUs) User goes to Deleted users in Entra ID and is kept 30 days, then removed for good

Moving a user out of a synced OU deletes them in the cloud

To Entra ID, a user that leaves the sync scope looks exactly like a deleted user. Their mailbox and OneDrive go with them after 30 days. Move users between synced OUs only, or restore them from Deleted users if it happens by mistake.

Entra Connect also has an accidental delete guard: if one sync run would delete more than 500 objects it stops and waits for you. Don't turn that off.

docs.title: What can still be done in the cloud
docs.text:
Some things are not part of sync and are managed in Entra ID even for synced users:

  • Licence assignment, MFA methods and Conditional Access policies.
  • Cloud-only groups (Microsoft 365 groups, Teams).
  • Guest users and cloud-only admin accounts.

Keep admin accounts cloud-only

Use a separate cloud-only account (admin@contoso.onmicrosoft.com) for Global Administrator and similar roles, not a synced AD account. If AD is ever compromised, the attacker doesn't get your tenant too.

docs.title: Users that already exist in both places
docs.text:
If someone created alice@contoso.com by hand in Entra ID before you set up sync, Entra Connect tries to link it to the AD user with the same UPN or primary SMTP address. This is called a soft match. After the match, the cloud account becomes a synced account and AD wins from then on.

Soft match is blocked for accounts that hold admin roles, on purpose. Remove the role, let it sync, then add the role back (or better, keep admins cloud-only as above).

docs.title: Entra Cloud Sync instead of Connect Sync
docs.text:
Microsoft also offers Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync. Instead of a full sync server with its own database, you install a small provisioning agent on one or more domain-joined servers, and the sync configuration lives in the Entra admin center.

Entra Connect Sync Entra Cloud Sync What you install Full sync engine with SQL LocalDB Lightweight agent, install 2 or 3 for high availability Where you configure it Wizard on the server Entra admin center Sync interval 30 minutes About every 2 minutes Several disconnected AD forests Hard Easy Device sync (hybrid join), complex custom rules, very large directories Yes Limited

My rule of thumb: for a new, simple setup (one forest, users and groups, password hash sync) try Cloud Sync first because there is less to maintain. If you need hybrid-joined devices, custom sync rules, or another feature Cloud Sync doesn't cover yet, use Connect Sync. The two can run side by side on different OUs during a migration. Check Microsoft's current comparison page before deciding, because Cloud Sync gains features often.

The Cloud Sync setup in short:

  1. Entra admin center → Entra ID → Entra Connect → Cloud sync → Agents → download the agent.
  2. Install it on SYNC01 (and later a second server) and sign in as Hybrid Identity Administrator.
  3. Back in the portal: New configuration → AD to Microsoft Entra ID sync → pick bhry98.local.
  4. Scoping filters: select the Staff and Groups OUs. Turn on Password hash sync.
  5. Enable the configuration and use Provision on demand to test one user first.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Likely cause and fix Users show up as @contoso.onmicrosoft.com Their UPN suffix isn't a verified domain. Fix the UPN in AD (Step 1) and sync again AttributeValueMustBeUnique error Two objects have the same proxyAddresses or UPN. Find it with Get-ADUser -Filter "proxyAddresses -eq 'smtp:alice@contoso.com'" and fix the duplicate User is in AD but not in Entra ID Not in a synced OU, or filtered out. Check Synchronization Service Manager → Metaverse search Password works on-premises but not in the cloud Password hash sync off or failing. Check the Connect Sync health page and run Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta "This operation can't be performed because the object is synced" in the portal Expected. Edit that field in AD instead Sync stopped with too many deletes The accidental delete guard kicked in. Check what is being deleted before you allow it

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• AD stays the place where you create, change and disable users. Entra ID gets a copy.
  • Give users a routable UPN (@contoso.com) before the first sync.
  • Sync only the OUs you need, with password hash sync for sign-in.
  • Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta pushes changes right away; otherwise they go every 30 minutes.
  • Disable leavers in AD, keep admin accounts cloud-only, and be careful moving users between OUs.

docs.title: How to install Git
docs.text:
Before you start

Not sure what Git is, or how it differs from GitHub and GitLab? Read What is Git? GitHub vs GitLab vs Bitbucket compared first.

By the end of this guide you will have:

  • Git installed and on your PATH
  • Your name, email and default branch configured
  • An SSH key added to GitHub or GitLab
  • Your first repository cloned and a commit pushed

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Requirement Notes Windows 10/11, macOS 12+ or a Linux distribution Admin / sudo rights to install A GitHub or GitLab account For Step 4 and later

docs.title: Step 1: Install Git
docs.text:
WindowsmacOSUbuntu / DebianRHEL / Rocky / Alma / Fedora

Option A: winget (fastest)

winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget

Option B: installer

  1. Download Git for Windows from https://git-scm.com/downloads/win.
  2. Run the installer. The defaults are fine; the choices worth checking are:
    • Default editor: pick one you know (VS Code, Notepad++), not Vim if you've never used it.
    • Initial branch name: Override → main.
    • PATH: Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software (recommended).
    • Line endings: Checkout Windows-style, commit Unix-style (core.autocrlf=true).
  3. Close and reopen your terminal so the new PATH is loaded.

You also get Git Bash, a Linux-like shell that is handy for the commands in this guide.

# Option A: Apple's Command Line Tools (includes git)
xcode-select --install

# Option B: Homebrew, usually a newer version
brew install git

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git

# Optional: latest stable Git on Ubuntu
sudo add-apt-repository -y ppa:git-core/ppa
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git

sudo dnf install -y git

Check it:

git --version

git version 2.51.0

Any 2.4x or newer version is fine for everything in this guide.

docs.title: Step 2: Tell Git who you are
docs.text:
Every commit records an author. Use the same email as your GitHub/GitLab account so commits are linked to your profile.

git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global pull.rebase false          # merge on pull (the beginner-friendly default)
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"  # optional: VS Code as editor

Line endings, so Windows and Linux colleagues don't fight over every file:

WindowsmacOS / Linux 
git config --global core.autocrlf true

git config --global core.autocrlf input

Check everything:

git config --global --list

docs.title: Step 3: Create an SSH key
docs.text:
SSH keys let you push and pull without typing a password or token each time.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
# Press Enter to accept ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, then choose a passphrase

Start the agent and add the key so you only type the passphrase once:

Windows (PowerShell as Administrator)macOSLinux 
Get-Service ssh-agent | Set-Service -StartupType Automatic
Start-Service ssh-agent
ssh-add $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

docs.title: Step 4: Add the key to GitHub or GitLab
docs.text:
Copy the public key (the .pub file, never the private one):

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
GitHubGitLab

Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → paste, give it a name, Add SSH key.

ssh -T git@github.com

Hi your-user! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

Preferences (your avatar) → SSH Keys → Add new key → paste, Add key.

ssh -T git@gitlab.com          # or your self-hosted GitLab hostname

Welcome to GitLab, @your-user!

HTTPS instead of SSH?

Behind a corporate proxy that blocks port 22, use HTTPS URLs. Git for Windows and macOS include Git Credential Manager, which opens a browser login once and stores the token securely.

docs.title: Step 5: Clone, commit and push
docs.text:
Create an empty repository named hello-git on GitHub/GitLab, then:

git clone git@github.com:your-user/hello-git.git
cd hello-git
echo "# Hello Git" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"
git push -u origin main

Refresh the repository page: your README is there.

Done. Git is installed, configured, and connected to your Git hosting platform.

docs.title: Handy extras
docs.text:
# A readable history graph
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"
git lg

# Global ignore file for OS / IDE junk
printf ".DS_Store\nThumbs.db\n.idea/\n.vscode/\n" > ~/.gitignore_global
git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
git: command not found / 'git' is not recognized

The terminal was opened before installation. Close and reopen it. On Windows, check that C:\Program Files\Git\cmd is in your PATH.

Permission denied (publickey)

The key isn't loaded or isn't added to your account. Run ssh-add -l to list loaded keys and ssh -vT git@github.com to see which key is offered.

ssh: connect to host github.com port 22: Connection timed out

Port 22 is blocked. GitHub accepts SSH on port 443. Add this to ~/.ssh/config:

Host github.com
  Hostname ssh.github.com
  Port 443
  User git
Commits show the wrong name or are not linked to my profile

The email in git config user.email doesn't match an email on your account. Fix the config, or add that email to your GitHub/GitLab profile.

docs.text:

  • Pro Git book (free)

docs.title: How to install Keycloak
docs.text:
Keycloak is an open-source identity and access management server. It gives your applications single sign-on, OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect, user federation (LDAP, Active Directory) and role management, so your apps don't have to store passwords themselves.

By the end of this guide you will have:

  • Keycloak running locally
  • A realm, a client and a user
  • An access token returned by Keycloak

What you're setting up: apps send users to Keycloak to log in, and Keycloak stores everything in PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Version Needed for Docker or Podman any recent Options 1 and 2 OpenJDK 21 Option 3 (Linux, no containers) Free ports 8080, 9000 HTTP and health endpoints

Which option should I pick?

  • Option 1 is the quickest way to try Keycloak. Data is lost when the container is removed.
  • Option 2 keeps data in PostgreSQL and is the right base for a real server.
  • Option 3 runs Keycloak directly on a Linux machine without containers.

docs.title: Step 1: Install and start Keycloak
docs.text:
Option 1: Docker (quick start)Option 2: Docker Compose + PostgreSQLOption 3: Linux (no containers) 
docker run --name keycloak -p 8080:8080 -p 9000:9000 \
  -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin \
  -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin \
  -e KC_HEALTH_ENABLED=true \
  quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.4 start-dev

start-dev runs Keycloak in development mode: plain HTTP, relaxed settings and an embedded database. Use it for learning and local testing only.

Create a folder with this compose.yaml:

compose.yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: keycloak
      POSTGRES_USER: keycloak
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: change-me # (1)!
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U keycloak"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  keycloak:
    image: quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.4
    command: start-dev # (2)!
    environment:
      KC_DB: postgres
      KC_DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/keycloak
      KC_DB_USERNAME: keycloak
      KC_DB_PASSWORD: change-me
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME: admin
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD: admin
      KC_HEALTH_ENABLED: "true"
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
      - "9000:9000"
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  pgdata:
  1. Use a strong password, ideally from a .env file that is not committed to git.
  2. Switch to start for production, see Going to production.

Start both containers:

docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f keycloak

# 1. Java 21 (RHEL / Fedora shown; use apt on Debian / Ubuntu)
sudo dnf install -y java-21-openjdk

# 2. Download and extract Keycloak
KC_VERSION=26.4.0
curl -LO https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/download/${KC_VERSION}/keycloak-${KC_VERSION}.tar.gz
tar -xzf keycloak-${KC_VERSION}.tar.gz
cd keycloak-${KC_VERSION}

# 3. Start in development mode with a temporary admin user
export KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin
export KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin
bin/kc.sh start-dev --health-enabled=true

Tip

Check the Keycloak releases page for the latest version number and change KC_VERSION.

Wait for a log line similar to:

Keycloak 26.4.0 on JVM (powered by Quarkus) started in 6.512s. Listening on: http://0.0.0.0:8080

docs.title: Step 2: Check that Keycloak is healthy
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:9000/health/ready

Expected output:

{ "status": "UP", "checks": [] }

docs.title: Step 3: Log in to the admin console
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:8080/admin and sign in with admin / admin.

Temporary admin

The bootstrap admin is meant to be temporary. After your first login, create a permanent admin user in the master realm and delete the bootstrap one.

docs.title: Step 4: Create a realm
docs.text:
A realm is an isolated space with its own users, clients and settings. Keep master for administering Keycloak and create a separate realm for your applications.

  1. Click the realm dropdown at the top left (it shows master).
  2. Click Create realm.
  3. Set Realm name to demo and click Create.

docs.title: Step 5: Create a client
docs.text:
A client is an application that asks Keycloak to authenticate users.

  1. In the demo realm, go to Clients → Create client.
  2. Client type: OpenID Connect, Client ID: demo-app, then Next.
  3. Leave Client authentication off (a public client) and enable Direct access grants so we can test with curl in Step 7. Click Next.
  4. Valid redirect URIs: http://localhost:3000/* (your app's URL), then Save.

Note

Direct access grants (the password grant) are used here only to test quickly. Real web apps should use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE.

docs.title: Step 6: Create a user
docs.text:
1. Go to Users → Create new user.
  2. Username: alice, fill in email, first and last name, then Create.
  3. Open the Credentials tab → Set password, enter a password and turn Temporary off.

docs.title: Step 7: Get an access token
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/realms/demo/protocol/openid-connect/token \
  -d grant_type=password \
  -d client_id=demo-app \
  -d username=alice \
  -d password='your-password' | jq

You should get back an access_token, a refresh_token and an expires_in value. Paste the access token into https://jwt.io to see its claims: iss, preferred_username, realm_access and so on.

Done. Keycloak is running and issuing tokens for your realm.

docs.title: Going to production
docs.text:
start-dev is not for production. For a real server, use start and configure a hostname and TLS:

Keycloak terminates TLSBehind a reverse proxy (Nginx, OpenShift route) 
bin/kc.sh start \
  --hostname=https://sso.example.com \
  --https-certificate-file=/etc/keycloak/tls.crt \
  --https-certificate-key-file=/etc/keycloak/tls.key \
  --db=postgres --db-url=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/keycloak \
  --db-username=keycloak --db-password=change-me

bin/kc.sh start \
  --hostname=https://sso.example.com \
  --proxy-headers=xforwarded \
  --http-enabled=true \
  --db=postgres --db-url=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/keycloak \
  --db-username=keycloak --db-password=change-me

Production checklist:

  • Use PostgreSQL (or another supported database), never the embedded dev database
  • Serve Keycloak over HTTPS only
  • Replace the bootstrap admin with a permanent admin account
  • Keep the management port 9000 internal (health and metrics only)
  • Back up the database regularly

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Port 8080 is already in use

Map a different host port, for example -p 8180:8080, and open http://localhost:8180.

HTTPS required error when logging in

The master realm requires HTTPS for non-local addresses. Use localhost while testing, or set up TLS as shown in Going to production.

invalid_grant or unauthorized_client from the token endpoint

Check that Direct access grants is enabled on the client, the username and password are right, and the password is not marked Temporary.

docs.text:

  • Keycloak Laravel Auth for Laravel applications
  • Official Keycloak server guides

docs.title: How to install Nginx
docs.text:
Before you start

New to Nginx? Read What is Nginx and why do we use it? first. It explains what a reverse proxy, load balancer and TLS termination are, which makes this guide and the next one much easier to follow.

This guide installs Nginx Open Source from the official nginx.org repository (newer than most distribution packages), starts it as a service and checks that it serves a page.

By the end of this guide you will have:

  • Nginx installed and running as a service
  • Port 80 open in the firewall
  • Your own page served from /var/www/example
  • Know where the configuration files and logs are

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Notes A Linux server, a Docker host or a Windows machine Ubuntu 22.04/24.04, Debian 12, RHEL/Rocky/Alma 9 or 10, Fedora sudo access Linux options Free port 80 (and 443 later) Stop Apache/IIS first if they use it

Stable or mainline?

Nginx publishes two branches. Stable (even minor number, e.g. 1.28.x) only receives critical fixes. Mainline (odd number, e.g. 1.29.x) gets new features first. For servers, choose stable. It is the same idea as LTS, explained in What does LTS mean?

docs.title: Step 1: Install Nginx
docs.text:
Ubuntu / DebianRHEL / Rocky / Alma / FedoraDocker / PodmanWindows 
# 1. Tools needed to add the repository
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y curl gnupg2 ca-certificates lsb-release

# 2. Import the official nginx signing key
curl -fsSL https://nginx.org/keys/nginx_signing.key \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nginx-archive-keyring.gpg

# 3. Add the stable repository (use "debian" instead of "ubuntu" on Debian)
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nginx-archive-keyring.gpg] \
http://nginx.org/packages/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) nginx" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nginx.list

# 4. Install
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y nginx

Quick option

sudo apt install nginx without steps 1 to 3 also works, but installs the (older) version packaged by Ubuntu/Debian with a slightly different layout (sites-available/).

# 1. Add the official stable repository
sudo tee /etc/yum.repos.d/nginx.repo > /dev/null <<'EOF'
[nginx-stable]
name=nginx stable repo
baseurl=http://nginx.org/packages/centos/$releasever/$basearch/
gpgcheck=1
enabled=1
gpgkey=https://nginx.org/keys/nginx_signing.key
module_hotfixes=true
EOF

# 2. Install
sudo dnf install -y nginx

On Fedora, simply run sudo dnf install -y nginx (Fedora already ships recent versions).

docker run -d --name nginx -p 8080:80 \
  -v "$PWD/html:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro" \
  nginx:stable-alpine

Put an index.html in ./html and open http://localhost:8080. With Docker you can skip Steps 2 and 3. If containers are new to you, read Containers vs traditional deployment.

OpenShift / rootless

On OpenShift use nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged, which listens on 8080 and runs as a non-root user.

  1. Download the Stable version zip from https://nginx.org/en/download.html.
  2. Extract it to C:\nginx.
  3. Start it from PowerShell:
cd C:\nginx
start nginx
tasklist /fi "imagename eq nginx.exe"   # you should see two nginx.exe processes

Stop it with .\nginx.exe -s stop, reload config with .\nginx.exe -s reload.

Warning

Nginx for Windows is fine for development and testing, but it is not built for production traffic (it uses select() and one worker). Use Linux for real servers.

Check the installed version:

nginx -v

nginx version: nginx/1.28.0

docs.title: Step 2: Start Nginx and enable it at boot
docs.text:
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx --no-pager

You should see active (running).

docs.title: Step 3: Open the firewall
docs.text:
firewalld (RHEL family)ufw (Ubuntu) 
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full'   # or: sudo ufw allow 80,443/tcp
sudo ufw status

SELinux (RHEL / Rocky / Fedora)

SELinux stays enforcing. Don't disable it. If Nginx must proxy to an app port later, allow it with sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1. If you serve files from a custom folder, label it: sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/var/www(/.*)?" && sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www.

docs.title: Step 4: Check the default page
docs.text:
curl -I http://localhost

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx/1.28.0
Content-Type: text/html

Open http://<server-ip>/ in a browser and you should see Welcome to nginx!

docs.title: Step 5: Serve your own site
docs.text:
Create the content:

sudo mkdir -p /var/www/example
echo '<h1>Hello from Nginx</h1>' | sudo tee /var/www/example/index.html

Create a server block. With the nginx.org packages, every *.conf file in /etc/nginx/conf.d/ is loaded automatically:

/etc/nginx/conf.d/example.conf
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name example.local;      # your domain or the server IP

    root  /var/www/example;
    index index.html;

    access_log /var/log/nginx/example.access.log;
    error_log  /var/log/nginx/example.error.log;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
    }
}

Test the configuration, then reload without dropping connections:

sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx
curl -H "Host: example.local" http://localhost

<h1>Hello from Nginx</h1>

Done. Nginx is installed, starts at boot and serves your site.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
Path What it is /etc/nginx/nginx.conf Main configuration (workers, logging, include lines) /etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf Your server blocks (nginx.org packages, RHEL) /etc/nginx/sites-available/ + sites-enabled/ Server blocks on Debian/Ubuntu distro packages /usr/share/nginx/html Default welcome page /var/log/nginx/access.log, error.log Logs

Useful commands:

sudo nginx -t                 # test config (always before reload)
sudo nginx -T                 # print the full, merged configuration
sudo systemctl reload nginx   # apply config with zero downtime
sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (98: Address already in use)

Another program uses port 80 (often Apache or another Nginx). Find it with sudo ss -ltnp | grep ':80 ', stop it, then start Nginx again.

403 Forbidden

Nginx can't read the files. Check permissions (namei -l /var/www/example/index.html), make sure there is an index.html, and on RHEL check the SELinux label (see Step 3).

Works with curl localhost but not from another machine

The firewall (Step 3) or a cloud security group is blocking port 80.

502 Bad Gateway when proxying to an app

The backend app is not running or not reachable. On RHEL, also run sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1.

docs.text:
